Creation of a Gene Bank 
*322. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any proposal to create a gene bank for 
private and public organisations; 
(b) if so, the modalities worked out in this regard so far; and 
(c) the funds allocated for the current Five Year Plan for this purpose? 
 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Government has already established National 
Gene Banks for Microbes, Blue Gr een Algae, Marine Cyanobacteria, 
Medicinal & Aromatic Plants, Drosophiia, Filarial Parasites, Seeds for food 
and agricultural crops, etc. These Gene Banks which are being supported by the 
Ministry of Science and Technology, (Department of Biotechnology, Council 
of Scientific and Industrial Research) and Indian Council of Agricultural 
Research, are accessible to public and private sector organizations for utilizing 
the genetic material as per their requirement. Setting up of more gene 
banks/repositories would depend upon the needs and requirements of scientists, 
institutions and industry engaged in research, production and trade. 
(c) A total amount of Rs. 46.28 Crores has been allocated for the current 
five year plan for these Gene Banks, where Department of Biotechnology, 
Council of Scientific and Industrial Research and Indian Council of 
Agricultural Research have allocated Rs. 15.84, Rs. 4.00 and Rs. 26.44 Crores 
respectively. 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Sir, the technology, more particularly 
bio-technology, scientific and industrial research, apart from agricultural 
research are very essential for all round development of our country; and to 
compete with the developed countries we  need to encourage our research and 
scientific fraternity to achieve our goals. In this background, I would like to 
know from the hon. Minister how far the gene banks established in our 
country are useful for the scientists and the common man of our country? Is 
there any intellectual audit in various scientific organisations of our country? 
If so, what are the details?

SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I think, it is the obligation of 
every country to, in fact, establish gene banks to protect its bio-diversity. With 
that in mind we have established gene  banks in various areas from medicinal 
and aromatic plants to seeds in agricultural produce to blue and green algae, 
cyanobacteria, a range of things to prot ect our biodiversity. In fact, we have 
one international depository authority as well, which is Institute of Molecular 
Technology, IMTECH, which is situated in Chandigarh, which accords to 
international standards. In the Ministry of Agriculture, we have, in fact 
accessions of 3,00,000, which is probably the largest in Asia. So, we are taking 
care of our gene banks. We need to make much better efforts at this and we have, 
in fact, written to the various Departments of Government of India under various 
Ministries to establish international depository authorities. Certainly, audits are 
taking place. Basically a gene bank is a service agency. So, we are servicing all 
in the private sector and the public sect or; whenever they want any particular 
micro-organism, we supply to them and that really is the basic purpose of a 
gene bank.

they

Statement 
(a) For assisting eligible applicants in setting up agro and rural 
industries, the Central Government implements the Rural Employment 
Generation Programme (REGP) and Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana 
(PMRY). Under both these programmes, loans are provided to eligible 
applicants by banks and subsidy by the Government. The State/Union 
Territory (UT)-wise details of investment made under REGP and PMRY 
during 2002-03, 2003-04, 2004-05 and 2005-06 (upto September 2005) 
are given in the enclosed Statement-I and Statement-ll, respectively, (See 
below). 
(b) The problems of agro and rural industries include use of obsolete 
technology, inconsistent quality of products, products not being in tune with 
the market demand, inadequate and delayed credit, management deficiencies, 
etc. 
(c) The primary responsibility of promoting small scale industries (SSI), 
including agro and rural industries, re sts with the State/LIT Governments. 
However, the Central Government implements a number of schemes to 
supplement the efforts of the State/UT Government. Some of the important 
schemes are: 
(i) Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS) for technology 
upgradation and modernisation of production techniques; 
(ii) Small Industry Cluster Development Programme (SICDP) for 
holistic development of SSI clusters; 
(iii) Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Small Industries for providing 
guarantee cover to banks for collateral-free loans upto Rs. 25 lakh; 
(iv) Rural Industries Service Cent res (RISC) Scheme for setting up of 
common facility centres (CFCs) to provide infrastructural support 
and services to such industries; 
(v) Product Development, Design Intervention and Packaging (PRODIP) 
Scheme for improved design and packaging of village industry 
products; 
(vi) Financial assistance to village industry units for participation in 
national and international level exhibitions for market development;

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2005] 
Statement 
(a) The latest information on State-wise teledensity (rural and urban areas) i.e. upto 
31.10.2005 is given in the enclosed Statement-I (See below). 
(b) and (c) Yes Sir. The rural teledensity has been lower than the urban tele-density 
because the development of network was more urban centric, particularly in the Private 
Sector. Higher economic and literacy status in the urban areas were also contributing 
factors. 
(d) A number of steps have been taken by the Government to increase the 
telephone density in rural areas which include the following: 
(i) Setting up of the USO Fund by the Government for provision of telephones 
in the rural areas; 
(ii) Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) has relaxed the distance for laying 
outdoor cables from 2.5 Kms. to 5 Kms. for Landline Exchanges which would facilitate 
larger coverage in the rural areas from existing exchanges; and 
(iii) Increased provision of WLL (Wireless in Local Loop) phones by BSNL.

*327. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state:

Statement 
(a) to (c) The July 18,2005 understanding on India-US civil nuclear 
energy cooperation agreed by India and the United States of America. The 
elements of this understanding as contained in the Joint Statement are as 
follows:— 
* President Bush conveyed his appreciation to the Prime Minister over 
India's strong commitment to preventing WMD proliferation and stated 
that as a responsible state with advanced nuclear technology, India 
should acquire the same benefits and advantages as other such States. The 
US President told the Prime Minister that he would work to achieve full 
civil nuclear energy cooperation with India as it realizes its goals of 
promoting nuclear power and achieving energy security. 
* The US President would also seek agreement from the US Congress to adjust 
U.S. laws and policies, and the United States will work with friends and 
allies to adjust international regimes to enable full civil nuclear energy 
cooperation and trade with India, including but 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2005] 
not limited to expenditious consideration of fuel supplies for 
safeguarded nuclear reactors at Tara pur. In the meantime, the United 
States will encourage its partners to also consider this request expeditiously. 
* India has expressed its interest in ITER and a willingness to contribute. 
The United States will consult with its partners considering India's 
participation. 
* The United States will consult with the other participants in the 
Generation IV International Forum with a view towards India's 
inclusion. 
* The Prime Minister conveyed that for its part, India would reciprocally 
agree that it would be ready to assume the same responsbilities and 
practices and acquire the same benefits and advantages as other leading 
countries with advanced nuclear technology, such as the United States. 
These responsibilities and practices consist of: 
 
■ identifying and separating civilian and military nuclear facilities and 
programmes in a phased manner and filing a declaration regarding its 
civilian facilities with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA); 
■ taking a decision to place voluntarily its civilian nuclear facilities 
under IAEA safeguards; signing a nd adhering to an Additional 
Protocol with respect to civilian nuclear facilities; 
■ continuing India's unilateral moratorium on nuclear testing; working 
with the United States for the conclusion of a multilateral Fissile 
Material Cut Off Treaty; 
■ refraining from transfer of enrichment and reprocessing 
technologies to States that do not have them and supporting 
international efforts to limit their spread; and 
■ ensuring that the necessary steps ha ve been taken to secure nuclear 
materials and technology through comprehensive export control 
legislation and through harmonization and adherence to Missile 
Technology Control Regime (MTCR) and Nuclear Suppliers Group 
(NSG) guidelines. 
The implementation of the July 18 understanding would be guided fully 
and entirely by the commitments reflected in the Joint Statement

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) The earthquake of 8th October, 
2005 (occurred in Pakistan near Muzaffarabad), as referred to in the question, 
was widely felt in parts of northern States like Jammu and Kashmir (J&K), 
Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Delhi and Ra jasthan, etc. As per the information 
provided by Ministry of Home Affairs, a total number of 1,338 persons have 
lost their lives (1336 it) Jammu and Kashmir and 2 in Punjab). Over 39,000 
buildings/houses are reported to have been fully-damaged, while more than 
71,000 were reported to be partially damaged in the State of J&K. 
(b) As per the seismic zoning map published by Bureau of Indian 
Standard (BIS), the country has been divided into four seismic zones, 
namely, zone-ll-V. Zone-V is consider ed to be more seismically active, 
while zone-ll is the least. Accordingly to this classification, Delhi falls in 
zone-IV which can experience earthquake of intensity up to VIII on 
Modified Mercalli (MM) scale. The intensity at a given place depends on 
the magnitude and distance of the ear thquake epicenter. Delhi can be 
affected by strong earthquakes occurring in the highly earthquake prone 
regions in Himalaya besides local earthquakes of small to moderate 
magnitudes. As per intensity VIII of MM scale the maximum damage that 
can occur to structures in Delhi due to earthquakes is as follows:. 
(i) Slight in specially designed structures 
(ii)        Considerable in ordinary buildings 
(iii)       Very heavy in poorly built structures 
A study of microzonation of Delhi has recently been completed at 
1:50,000 scale, which shows that within the city of Delhi itself the impact of an 
earthquake may not be uniform over the city due to varying properties of the soil and 
geological characteristics. However, at this stage it is difficult to say how safe is 
Delhi from earthquakes. 
(c) to (e) Based on the present st andards prescribed by BIS, the

and Country Planning Legislation, Zoning Regulation Development Control 
and Building Regulation/Bye-laws for Safety against earthquakes have been 
prepared by an Expert Committee constituted by the Ministry of Home Affairs,

to meet the requirements of the States. Microzonation of urban areas may lead to

Uranium Deposits 
2426. SHRIMATI S. G. INDIRA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has tied up the medium term fuel 
supplies for nuclear energy programme of generating 13,000 m.w. of power; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that country is developing Indigenous air borne 
survey instruments to locate more deposits of Uranium; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTERS OFFICE 
(SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAV AN): (a) and (b) Present nuclear programme 
envisages reaching 13000 MWe generation capacity by 2013. We expect this 
capacity to be made up of a mix of Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs), 
Light Water Reactors (LWRs) and Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs). While fuel 
for PHWRs would be supplied from indigenous mines, fuel for LWRs would 
need to be imported. FBR would run on recycled fuel materials. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) India is developing Air Borne Survey instruments indigenously to 
locate more deposits of Uranium. The development is done jointly by various 
constituent R&D Units and PSU of this Department as well as other 
institutions. The system being developed is called Airborne Time Domain 
Electromagnetic Survey System with a ca pability to identify the presence of 
uranium deposits located below ground level.

operators in 2003; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the action plan of Government to 
reserve the trend? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) and (b) The rural tele-density as on March 1999 was 
0.52 as compared to urban tele-density of 2.3. As on 30th September, 2005 the 
rural tele-density has increased to 1.77 as compared to urban tele-density of 
31.25. This is happening because the Telecom service providers (especially 
those in the private sector) are focusing more on urban areas because of higher 
revenue per line in urban areas as compared to that in rural areas. 
(c) and (d) The rural tele-density as on March 2003 was 1.49 as 
compared to urban tele-density of 14.32, whereas as on 30th September 2005 the 
rural tele-density has increased to 1.77 as compared to urban tele-density of 
31.25. 
To provide support for expansion of telegraph services Universal Service 
Obligation Fund (USOF) has been created w.e.f. 1.4.2002. Some of the activities 
for which support from USOF has been extended include: 
(i) Provision of Village Public Telephones (VPTs) in 66,822 
remaining unconnected villages excluding villages having 
population less than 100, lying in thick forest area/naxalite infested 
areas etc. by November 2007.14,233 VPTs have been provided as on 
31.10.2005. 
(ii) Provision of second VPT in the form of Rural Community Phones 
(RCPs) in villages having population of more than 2,000 and having no 
PCQ by September 2007. 15,946 RCPs have been provided as on 
30.09.2005. 
(iii) To provide Rural Phone Connectivity 'on demand' in 1,685 
commercially unviable Short Distance Charging Areas (SDCAs) by 
the first quarter of the year 2006.

Assessment of poverty line 
+2523. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the criteria for assessing a person or a family in the country 
living Below Poverty Line; 
 
(b) whether this assessment is done every year and in what way 
common people are informed about it; 
(c) whether any increase or decrease has been taking place every year in terms of 
the number of people living Below Poverty Line in the State of Rajasthan; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof, district-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI M. 
V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) Planning Commission uses per capita 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2005] 
consumption expenditure as the criterion for assessing a person living below 
poverty line in the country. This assessment is done for individuals and not for 
families. The Task Force on 'Minimum Needs and Effective Consumption 
Demands' (1979) fixed the per capita consumption norm at Rs. 49.09 per 
month in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 per month in urban areas at 1973-74 prices 
at national level, corresponding to a basket of goods and services anchored on 
a norm of per capita daily calorie requirement of 2400 kcal. in rural areas and 
2100 kcal. in urban areas, which also meets a minimum of non-food 
requirements, such as clothing, shelter, transport etc. The Task Force used the 
age-sex-activity specific calorie allowances recommended by the Nutrition 
Expert Group (1968) to estimate the average daily per capita requirement for 
rural and urban areas using the age-sex-occupational structure of their 
respective population (as projected for 1982-83). The per capita consumption 
expenditure fixed for State/UT for determination of the poverty line are 
derived from the national level per capita consumption expenditure, using State-
specific price indices and inter-State price differentials, according to the 
methodology given by Expert Group on 'Estimation of Proportion and Number 
of Poor' (Lakdawala Committee 1997). The prescribed per capita consumption 
expenditure limits for determination of people living below poverty line are 
updated using State-specific cost of living indices, that is, Consumer Price 
Indices for Agricultural Labourers (CPIAL) for rural areas and Consumer 
Price Indices for Industrial Workers (CPIIW) for urban areas. 
(b) Planning Commission's assessment on incidence of poverty, that is, 
estimates on percentage of population living below poverty line, at national 
and State level are based on the large sample survey on household consumer 
expenditure conducted by the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) 
at an interval of approximately five years. The latest estimates on population 
living below poverty line are available for the year 1999-2000 (NSS-55th 
Round). These estimates are made available to the public through press 
releases.

2542. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: W ill the Minister of SHIPPING, 
ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state :

fatal accidents involving Indian Seamen abroad foreign ships;

flag vessels who are being exploited by fly-by night shiplines;

HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir.

estimated to be around 50,000. Indian Maritime Administration is not 
controlling employment of Indian seafarers on foreign flag vessels.

Conventions etc. as applicable to the flag country. However, the Director

welfare of Indian seafarers on board foreig n flag ships. It may be difficult to

(b) The Comprehensive Policy for the Maritime Sectors (Ports, 
Merchant Shipping and IWT), which is at draft stage, seeks to combine vision 
and strategy for the sector through harmonious and coordinated development of 
country's maritime assets like ports, shipping, inland water transport systems and 
ship building and ship repair industries. The main points in the draft Policy are 
as follows*:— 
(i) Holistic development of maritime transport systems through a 
coordinated plan and strategies for development of port 
infrastructure, improvement in shipping, backward integration of the 
hinterland through rail, road and inland water transport 
connectivity, augmentation of ship building and ship repair 
facilities so as to emerge as an internationally competitive nation 
in this area by 2025.

(ii) Ensure quality service comparab le with international benchmarks 
in Indian port through modernization, improvement in 
productivity and structural reforms. 
(iii) Facilitate transhipment of Indian origin/bound cargo in Indian 
ports. 
(iv) Effect significant increase in Indian Shipping and IWT tonnage 
through facilitative policy interventions. 
(v) Promote coastal shipping and inland water transport through a 
package of measures including fiscal and financial incentives. 
(vi) Strengthen maritime administration and bring about regulatory 
framework reforms to promote good governance. 
(vii) Provide level playing field to Indian stakeholders by providing 
fiscal regime at par with intern ational norms and by rationalizing 
domestic levies. 
(viii) Provide for state- of-the-art aids to navigation and requisite 
regulatory framework. 
(ix) Encourage ship-building and sh ip-repair activities to become 
internationally competitive a nd emerge as a leading ship-
butkJing/fthip-repair nation by 2025. 
(x) Support ship-breaking and ship-recycling activities without 
compromising on environmental concerns. 
(xi) Stimulate private sector investment including foreign direct 
investment particularly for rendering services of a commercial 
nature in the Maritime sector, by providing conducive 
environment. 
(xii) Promote shipping-trade interface by evolving code of conduct for 
supply chain players such as freight forwarders, shipping agents, 
multimodal transport operators and other intermediaries. 
(xiii) Develop human resources in maritime sector and market them in the 
context of emerging global shortage of qualified personnel in the 
sector.

Credit delivery to SSI 
2563. DR. T SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: 
Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether better credit delivery to Small Scale Industry sector by RBI, 
State Financing Corporations and SIDBI are necessary for further enhancing 
role of small and medium enterprises; 
(b) whether in its report on national strategy for manufacturing 
National Manufacturing Competitiveness Council (NMCC) has 
recommended that a separate law for small enterprises including chapter on 
provisions of credit to SSIs be framed as prevalent in other countries; 
(c) whether some problems are being faced in accessing credit; and 
(d) if so, what steps considered by Government to remove such- 
hurdles that are being faced by SSI units? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) Yes, Sir. However, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) does not 
provide credit to the small scale industries (SSI) sector but formulates general 
policies for delivery of credit to the sector by banks, etc. 
209 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2005] 
(b) In its draft report on 'National Strategy for Manufacturing'. The 
National Manufacturing Competitiveness Council has recommended a 
separate law for small enterprises and made several observations on 
provision of credit to the SSI. 
(c) and (d) To facilitate flow of credit to the SSI units, the Government and 
the RBI have taken various measures which, inter alia include enhancement 
in composite loan limit from Rs. 50 lakh to Rs. 1 crore, raising of project cost 
limit under National Equity Fund (NEF) scheme from Rs. 25 lakh to Rs. 50 
lakh, enhancement of eligible loan limit under 
-Credit Guarantee Scheme from Rs. 10 lakh to Rs. 25 lakh, providing 
collaterial free loan upto Rs. 25 lakh to SSI units having good track record, setting 
up of Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) fund of Rs. 10,000 crore under 
Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI), enhancement of credit 
limit under Laghu Udhyami Credit Card (LUCC) from Rs. 2 lakh to Rs. 10 
lakh based on satisfactory track record, etc. 
Further, the Government has announced a 'Policy Package for Stepping 
up Credit to Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs)' on 10th August 2005. 
The measures in the Policy Package to increase the quantum of credit to SMEs 
(including SSIs) include: (i) public sector banks to fix their own targets for 
funding SMEs in order to achieve a minimum 20 per cent year-on-year growth 
in credit to the SME sector, (ii) public sector banks to follow a transparent 
rating system with cost of credit linked to the credit rating of the enterprises, 
(iii) commercial banks to make concerted efforts to provide credit cover on an 
average to at least 5 new tiny, small and medium enterprises at each of their 
semi-urban/ urban branches per year, (iv) special dispensation under the 
Credit Guarantee Scheme for all (a) loans upto Rs. 2 lakh, (b) eligible women 
entrepreneurs and (c) eligible borrowers located in the North Eastern region 
(including Sikkim) and Jammu and Kashmir, (v) adoption of cluster-based 
approach by banks for SME financing.

Closure of SSI units 
2565. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the major factors responsible for closure of small scale industrial units 
in different parts of the country; 
(b) the number of labourers rendered jobless due to its closure, 
category-wise along with steps taken to provide employment to these workers 
and technicians; 
(c) whether Government are aware that small scale industrialists are 
facing infrastructural/technical problems like Sales Tax, Income Tax, Electricity 
Boards, and State financial institutions; and 
212 

[15 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA  
(d) if so, the details thereof along with the action taked by Government 
in this regard for smooth functioning of these units? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHABIR PRASAD): (a) Though closure of a small scale industry (SSI) is 
dependent on the decision of the SSI concerned, some of the major factors 
responsible for closure of SSIs are fall in demand for specific products, 
change in technology, inadequacy of working capital, shortage of raw 
materials, marketing problems, lack  of competitiveness, management 
inadequacies, etc. 
(b) The date on the number of labourers rendered jobless due to 
closure of SSIs are not maintained  centrally. However, workers and 
technicians rendered jobless due to clos ure of SSI units can avail of the self-

order to solve the problems faced by SSI sector, relating to availability of 
credit, technology upgradation, infra structure and marketing facilities, the 
Central Government also implements a number of schemes/programmes to 
supplement these efforts.    . 
Disaster Management support system 
2566. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Department of Space has evolved a 
space based disaster management support system; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether this system had been put to use during the recent natural 
disasters in the country; and 
(d) if so, the extent of success achieved as a result of it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE 
(SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2005] 
Space based disaster management supp ort system being implemented by 
Department of Space, jointly with Ministry of Home Affairs, comprises of 
the following elements: 
— Creation of digital database, for disaster-prone areas, towards 
facilitating hazard zonation and damage assessment; 
monitoring of major natural disasters using satellite and aerial 
data, and development of related techniques and tools. 
— Strengthening the communica tions backbone for timely 
dissemination of information and emergency support. 
— Setting up of a secure satellite based communication network 
linking the National Control Room at Ministry of Home Affairs 
with State Control Rooms and other concerned organizations. 
— Establishment of a Decision Support Centre at National Remote 
Sensing Agency (NRSA) of Department of Space, at Hyderabad, 
towards facilitating the disaster management operations by 
Ministry of Home Affairs. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The system had been put to use during the recent 
floods, tsunami, agricultural drought, earthquake, landslides and forest fires. 
Major flood events that occurred  during 2005 were monitored, 
mapped, and the information was furnished to the Ministry of Home affairs, 
Central Water Commission, and Relief Commissioner of the concerned 
States. The flood inundation information provided in near real time has been 
found to be useful for organizing relief operations and assessment of the 
damages. 
The artificial lake formed on the Pareechu River in the Tibetan region 
during July-August 2004, with threats of flash floods downstream in 
Himachal Pradesh, was monitored regularly till June 2005 and the 
information was provided to Ministry of Home Affairs for alert and 
necessary action. 
The post-tsunami relief, rehabilitati on and reconstruction efforts were 
supported by way of providing satellite phones for emergency 
214 

[15 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
communication, enabling telemedicine facilities and videoconferencing for 
rescue of the displaced people, da mage assessment and development of 
integrated cadastral level information in selected areas. 
The damage assessment due to th e recent earthquake in Jammu & 
Kashmir in October 2005 was carried out, and information was sent to 
Ministry of Home Affairs for relief and rehabilitation activities. 
During the 2005 Kharif season, mild agricultural drought was observed 
in parts of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and 
Uttar Pradesh. The agricultural drought information was sent to Ministry of 
Agriculture and the concerned State Agriculture Departments towards 
planning relief and contingency measures. The drought information is being 
used regularly by Ministry of Agriculture and State Departments of 
Agriculture to pursue drought management activities. 
Forest fire information derived from satellite data, on regular basis, is 
disseminated through the web site of NRSA of Department of Space.

Disaster warning set up in States 
2569. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the role of the disaster warning set up in each State, so far; 
(b) the amount spent for the purpose especially in Andhra Pradesh; 
(c) whether Government had taken the assistance of foreign firms with 
regard to the latest system in the process;     , 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) The question appears to 
refer to the Early Warning System for Tsunami and Storm Surges in Indian 
Ocean. As far as the Tsunami Warning System is concerned the Government is 
setting up an Early Warning System for Tsunami and Storm Surges in Indian 
Ocean at the total cost of Rs. 125 Crores with the following components:— 
• strengthening of the existing seismological network to indicate, near 
real time occurrence of tsunamigenic earthquakes; 
• Installation of tsunami warning sensors close to the ocean-bottom at 
appropriate locales in the In dian Ocean, with real time 
connectivity; 
• Tide gauge and data buoys networking to validate arrival of tsunami 
waves at the coast; 
• Modelling of the inundation scenarios for the entire coast and 
mapping of potential risk areas; 
• Collection of information, analysis and generating status 
advisories. 
A Centre would be set up at Indian National Centre for Ocean 
Information Services (ICOIS), Hyderabad,  Andhra Pradesh on a 24x7 basis. 
The system is scheduled to be operationalised by September, 2007. The Tsunami 
Warning System is for the whole country. 
221 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2005] 
(c) to (e) There is no assistance taken from foreign firms, however, the 
Indian system is the best system for our country.

last twenty years. Survey for construction of this line was completed in

*343     SHRI SANJAY RAUT:† 
SHRI TARIQ  ANWAR: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether heavy rains and floods in Maharashtra have caused extensive 
damage to onion crop in Maharashtra, if so, the extent of loss and damage 
to the crop; 
(b) what percentage of demand for onion in the country is met by 
Maharashtra, and how far the recent onion crisis in the country was 
attributable to this damage; and 
(c) what Central aid, if any, was sought and given to the Government of 
Maharashtra to help the farmers out of the crisis caused by such damage 
to onion crop? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to 
(c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.The question was actually 
asked on the floor of the House by Shri Sanjay Raut 
1 
 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December 2005] 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Heavy rains and floods in Maharashtra have caused extensive 
damage to onion crops during this year (2005). During April-May, 2005, 
unseasonal rain and high temperature during harevesting time of rabi crop 
resulted in poor quality which was responsible for reduced shelf-life because 
of which quantity of onion stored, decr eased by 25% in comparison to last 
year. Against 7 lakh tonnes stored in 2004, only 5.25 lakh tonnes could be 
stored in 2005. During July 2005, owing to continuous rains in Maharashtra, 
there was damage to the seed sown during early kharif, forcing the farmers to 
re-sow, causing production loss and delayed kharif crop in Maharashtra by 
about a month. Loss of nursery and delayed monsoon resulted in reduction of 
onion cropped area by about 15%. Again, during October, 2005, heavy rains 
damaged the kharif crop in some of the districts of Maharashtra. The overall 
loss in kharif production in Maharashtra is estimated to be about 43%. 
Against the production of 2.70 lakh tonnes in Khariff 2004, the production in 
Maharashtra during kharif, 2005 is 1.55 lakh tonnes. 
The State of Maharashtra meets 28% of  the total demand of onion in the 
country. As mentioned above, the unseasonal and excess rainfall is 
responsible for shortage in availability of onion and consequent price hike. 
This situation prevailed for a short period during the month of October 2005, 
which soon stabilized due to sufficient arrival of onion from Rajasthan and 
other Southern States. 
Government of Maharashtra submitted a memorandum to the Central 
Government for the floods that occurred in July-August, 2005 indicating the 
total agricultural loss at Rs. 1239.57 crore. Memorandum of the State 
Government did not indicate crop-wise breakup of the losses. Government 
have approved release of an amount of Rs. 697.45 crore.

Price control on drugs 
*346. SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: W ill the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are planning to ease control on pricing of drugs 
manufactured in India; and 
(b) whether Government studied the position that would arise by relaxing 
the control on drugs prices after which the drugs will become costlier for the 
consumers? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) and (b) A Statem ent is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) As per the present Pharma Pricing Policy, the 74 bulk drugs 
specified in the First Schedule of th e Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 
(DPCO, 95) and the formulations based thereon are under price control and 
their prices are fixed/revised by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing 
Authority (NPPA) in accordance with the provisions of the DPCO, 95. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the vari ous factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product  quality etc. The NPPA monitors 
the prices of medicines as per monthly Retail Audit Reports of ORG-IMS 
Research Pvt. Ltd. The Government takes corrective measures where the 
public interest is found to be adversely affected. 
The Government announced the 'Pharmaceutical Policy 2002' in February 
2002. However, a public interest litigation filed in the High Court of 
Karnataka at Bangalore resulted in an Order dated 12.11.2002 from Hon'ble 
High Court, which stopped the Government from implementing the price 
control regime envisaged in the Pharmaceutical Policy 2002. This 
Department filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) before the Supreme Court 
of India against the Order of the Ka rnataka High Court, which has been 
admitted as SLP (C) No. 3668/2003. The Supreme Court vide its order dated 
10.3.2003 directed the Government, inter-alia, that, "we suspend the 
operation of the order to the extent it directs that the Policy dated 15.2.2002 
shall not be implemented. However we direct that the petitioner 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
shall consider and formulate appropri ate criteria for ensuring essential and 
life saving drugs not to fill out of the price control and further directed to 
review drugs, Which are essential a nd lite saving in nature till 2nd May, 
2003". ministry of Health and Family Welfare has brought out the National 
List of Essential Medicines, 2003 after the review of the National Essential 
Drugs List, 1996. The matter is sub-judice before the Supreme Court. 
The National Common Minimum Programme as adopted by the 
Government aims, inter-alia, to ensure availability of life saving drugs at 
reasonable prices. In the light of National Common Minimum Programme 
and the observations of the Supreme Court in SLP (C) No. 3668/2003, the 
Government constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of Joint 
Secretary (PI) to suggest measures fo r fulfilling the objectives of National 
Common Minimum Programme to ensure the availability of life saving drugs 
at reasonable prices. This Committee has submitted its interim report to the 
Government. 
Subsequently, a Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, 
Principal Adviser, Planning Commission was constituted to explore options 
other than price control to make available life saving drugs at reasonable 
prices. During its meetings, the Task Fo rce deliberated upon almost all the 
recommendations made in its interim Report by the Committee under the 
Chairmanship of Joint Secr etary. The Task Force has submitted its report to 
the Government on the 20th September, 2005. Some of the salient 
recommendations of Task Force regarding the price management are, that 
Price Controls should be imposed on the 'essentiality' of the drug and not on 
the basis of turnover and its should be applied only to formulations and not to 
bulk drugs to promote generic drugs, to establish price negotiation process 
for new patented drugs, to streamline the bulk procurement regime, to 
exempt the excise duty, customs duty and other levies on cancer and anti 
HIV/AIDS drugs, to reduce the excise duty on drugs from 16 to 8%, to 
enhance the exemption limit of SSI units from Rs. 1 Crores to Rs. 5 Crores 
etc. 
A Core Group under the Chairmanship  of Joint Secretary (PI) has been 
constituted by this Department to examine the recommendations of the Task 
Force and to draft a new Pharmaceutical Policy. The Government is also in 
consultation with various stakeholders is examining the raoornmendations of 
the Task Force. Based on this a new Pharmaceutical Policy 
10

Is likely to be announced shortly. The main objective of the 
pharmaceutical policy will be to ensure availability of the life saving drugs 
and essential drugs at reasonable prices.

Statement 
The salient features of the National Steel Policy 
• The NSP sets out a broad roadmap for the Indian Steel Industry in its 
journey towards reform, restructing adn globalization. 
• The long-term goal of the NSP is that India should have a modern and 
efficient steel industry of world standards, catering to diversified steel 
damand. The focus of the policy is to achieve global competitiveness 
not only in terms of cost, quality and product-mix but also in terms of 
global benchmarks of efficiency and productivity. This will require 
indegenous production of 110 million tonnes per annum by 2019-20 
from the 2004-05 level of 38 million tonnes. This implies a 
compounded annual growth of 7.3 percent per annum. 
• In order to achieve the goal of 110 million tonnes of steel production 
by 2019-20, the country would require 190 million tonnes of iron ore 
and 70 million tonnes of coking coal. The NSP seeks to remove the 
supply-side constraints to the growth of this industry in an open, 
globally integrated and competitive enviornment. 
• The NSP seeks adopt a multi-pronged strategy to move towards the 
long-term policy goal. On the demand side, the strategy would be to 
create incremental demand through promotional efforts, creation of 
awareness and strengthening the deliv ery chain, particularly in rural 
areas. On the supply side, the strategy would be to facilitate 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
creation of additional capacity, remove procedural and policy 
bottlenecks in the availability of inputs such as iron ore and coal, make 
higher investments in R&D an d encourage the creation of 
infrastructure such as roads, railways, and ports. 
• The NSP targets a per capita consumption level of about 165kg. In 
urban areas and 4kg. in rural areas by 2019-20 as compared to 77kg. 
and 2 kg., respectively in 2004-05. The industry will be encouraged to 
set up new block level rural stock points in order to boost steel 
consumption. Measures will be taken to incorporate steel structures in 
the CPWD code for goverment buildin gs and to include steel usage in 
the curricula for technical institutes. 
• In order to achieve the strategic goal of 110 million tonnes of steel 
production by 2019-20, the industry would need additional capital Rs. 
2,30,000 crores. In addition, funds would be required for technological 
upgrade of existing facilities. 
• in order to mobilize such vast resources NSP seeks to encourage 
foreign direct investment. In addition the policy also seeks to devise 
suitable fiscal incentives for the steel industry. 
• The NSP seeks to support development of risk-hedging instruments 
like futures and derivatives to contain price volatility in the steel 
market. 
• The NSP seeks to strengthen the existing training and research 
facilities available to the domestic steel industry so as to provide 
suitable training programmes especi ally for the secondry small-scale 
units and also to collect and analy ze data on important parameters of 
the industry. 
• The NSP seeks to mount aggressive R&D efforts to create 
manufacturing capability for special types of steel, substitute coking 
coal, use iron ore fines, develop new products suited to rural needs, 
enhance material and energy efficiency, utilize waste, and arrest 
environmental degradation. 
• The NSP acknowledges the important role played by the secondary 
steel sector in providing employment, meeting local demand of steel in 
rural and semi-urban areas, and meeting thecountry's demand of some 
special products and seeks to endeavour to provide the 
18

necessary feedstock to these units at reasonable prices from major 
plants through the existing mechan ism of State Small Industries 
Corporations. 
  The NSP recognizes the fact that  integration of the Indian steel 
industry with the global economy requires that the industry should be 
protected from unfair trade practices, which become common 
especially during periods of downturn. The NSP therefore, envisages 
institution of mechanisms for important surveillance, and monitoring 
export subsidies in other countries.

*344. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND

(a) whether any target for taking health care to all parts of the country has 
been fixed;

will be required for 'Health-care for All project? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRYOF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKALAKSHMI): (a) and (b) 
The National Health Policy, 2002, laid down the main objective as achieving 
an acceptable standard of good health  amongst the general population of the 
country. This was targeted to be achieved by establishing new infrastructure 
in deficient area and by upgrading infrastructure in the existing institutions. 
Taking into account the gap in health  care facilities, National Health Policy, 
2002, envisages an increase in health s ector expenditure to 6% GDP with 2% 
of GDP being contributed as public health investment by the year 2010. 
The National Common Minimum Programme of the Government has also 
focused attention on increasing public investment in health. It is proposed to 
increase the expenditure in the health sector to the level of 2-3% of the GDP 
by increased contributions from the Central and State Governments. 
Towards this end, the Government has launched a National Rural Health 
Mission, which seeks to provide effect ive health care to rural population 
throughout the country with special focus on 18 States with poor health 
indicators and weak health infrastructure. The main objective is to provide 
accessible, affordable, accountable, ef fective and reliable health care, 
especially to poor and vulnerable sections of population with the ultimate 
objective to achieve Population Stabili zation Programme in the high fertility 
states of the country. Under the strategy of NRHM, the gap in the existing 
scenario of rural health care is to be addressed th rough 2.5 lakh Accredited 
Social Health Activists (ASHA) to assist the Anganwadi Worker and ANM at 
village level to make the increased h ealth services accessible to the rural 
people of the country. It is also proposed to upgrade CHCs to the level of 
India Public Health Standards (IPHS). NRHM has been launched for a period 
of 7 years (2005-2012) i.e. for two years of Tenth Plan and full Eleventh 
Plan.

lagging behind in farm mechanization and is promoting selective 
mechanisation. About 250 manual, animal and power operated equipment for

mechanization efforts in the country ha ve been made selectively for crops 
and their operations keeping in view the prevailing agro-socio-economic 
aspects. The mechanization in India is through an optimal blend of prevalent 
power sources i.e., manual, draft animals and mechanical. 
India is one of the largest producer of tractors in the world producing 
about 2.5 lakh tractors annually in the range of 20-75 hp. As of now there are

Decline in fish production 
*358. SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN:  Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there has been a great fall in  fish production especially wild 
stock from sea and rivers; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the corrective measures being unde rtaken to stimulate the fish 
production? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) 
Though the overall fish production from the country has been on the 
increase, marine fish production has been more or less steady at 28-29 lakh 
tonnes during 2000-2004 and has shown a slight fall to 27.8 lakh tonnes 
during 2004-05. There has been some fluctuation in riverine capture fisheries 
in the recent years. 
(b) The decline in marine fish production during 2004-05 is mainly 
attributed to the major havoc cause d by tsunami during December, 2004. 
Topographic changes due to construction of dams, bridges and barrages and 
increased land based pollution besides intensive fishing are the major reasons 
for decline in riverine capture fisheries. 
(c) In the marine sector resource conservation through closed seasons, 
mesh regulations and such other management measures are being 
implemented for replenishing the fish stock. Apart from this, production 
from the deep sea is being augmented by encouraging investment in the 
Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). Measur es to decongest the coastal waters 
by encouraging fishing beyond territorial waters by enabling the existing 
class of mechanised boats and encouraging introduction of the intermediate 
craft are being implemented. River ranching, abating pollution and fishing 
regulations are being practiced to enhance the health of riverine fish stock. 
Thrust is being given to increase fish production through aquaculture besides 
assisting the sector through various Central and Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes to improve fish production.

*359. SHRI NANDIYELLAIAH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND

Catheter is a hollow tube which is passed through the body of evacuating

oils. The studies suggest that formulation of policies in respect of calibration 
of import duties on edible oils, application of new technology to increase 
production and productivity in oil sector and provision of marketing support 
to oilseed farmers should be linked to the Indian proposals in the WTO 
Agriculture negotiations. Recently the Government has brought out a study 
entitled 'State of the Indian Farmer: A Millennium Study', as a part of which 
"Globalization and Agricultural Liberalization in India" has also been 
studied. Based on various measures of import and export competitiveness, 
the study concludes that most of the important agricultural commodities in 
India are competitive and that India can withstand competition from abroad 
with respect to the import of most of the crops, at the current levels of tariffs.

and supply, market position etc. The commercial scheme is aimed at creation 
of innovative market, value addition, harvesting, processing, storage and 
packaging. The contractual farming scheme aims at providing financial 
assistance to farmers for cultivation of medicinal plants with assured market 
on a large scale. The Board has sanctioned more than 2900 projects involving 
financial assistance of about Rs. 75.00 crores being implemented in different 
parts of the country during 2002-03,2003-04 and 2004-05. About 72,000 
acres land covered under cultivation of various prioritized medicinal plants.

sanctioned under promotion schemes. About 65,000 acres land has been 
covered under promotion schemes i nvolving activities like in-situ/ex-situ 
conservation and raising of herbal gard ens. 32 State Medicinal Plant Boards

2005-06 was fixed at 87.80 million tonnes which included 75.45 million 
tonnes of kharif rice and 12.35 million tonnes of rabi rice. Against the kharif 
target, the 1st advance estimates for th e 2005-06 put the estimated kharif rice 
production at 73.83 million tonnes which is 1.62 million short of the target. 
The reason for not achieving the target is mainly erratic behaviour of 
monsoon resulting in improper spatial and temporal distribution of rainfall.

irrigation. The Union Budget 2005-06 has provided Rs. 400 crore for 
promoting micro irrigation. The Accel erated Irrigation Benefit Programme 
was reviewed and an amount of Rs. 4,800 crore has been provided for the 
current year to complete the last mile projects without further delay.

rice include Integrated Cereals De velopment Programme in Rice Based 
Cropping Systems Areas (ICDP-Rice). From October, 2000, this scheme has 
been subsumed under Macro Management Programme with a view to 
provide flexibility to the States according to the regionally differentiated

2589. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA. Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE

(b)the details of areas that have been  identified in Andhra Pradesh which

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) The main objectives of the National 
Horticulture Mission (NHM) are:

based regionally differentiated strategies which include research, 
technology promotion, extension, post harvest management, 
73 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005]

Problem in agriculture sector 
†  2602. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
. Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have conducted a survey with regard to the 
problems being faced in the development of agriculture sector; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
96 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the main problems identified so far; 
(c) the problems out of the above which are due to paucity of funds; 
(d) the problems which are due to lack of knowledge; and 
(e) the decline noticed in agriculture sector due to the same? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (d) The National Sample Survey 
Organisation (NSSO), Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation 
conducted the Situation Assessment Survey of Farmers in 2003 covering 
different aspects like educational level of farmer households, level of living 
as measured by consumer expenditure and indebtedness, their farming 
practices and preferences, resource availability and their awarness of 
technological developments and access to modern technology. The areas of 
concern as found in the survey reports include high indebtedness of the 
farmer households, consumption level below the average of rural households, 
less accessibility to modern technology, poor awareness on certain important 
schemes like Minimum Support Pri ce and Crop Insurance and less 
participation in group activities through cooperative societies etc. 
(e) In India, agricultural growth is largely influenced by rainfall and 
climatic conditions since about 60 per cent area is still rain fed. The latest 
statistics released by Central Statistical Organisation shows that agricultural 
sector grew by 1.1 per cent during 2004-05 and the estimated average growth 
rate during the first two quarters of the current year i.e. 2005-06 is 2 per cent. 
Cotton production 
2603. SHRI PYARELAL  KHANDELWAL Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that over 230 lakh bales of cotton was produced in 
the cotton season 2004-05; 
(b) whether the cotton crop is expected to be over 270 lakh bales in the 
cotton season 2005-06 and whether this will affect the prices; 
(c) whether Government are contemplating to export surplus cotton; 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
(d) whether Government are aware that China will be short of cottion by 
almost 2.5 to 3 million metric tonnes in the cotton season 2005-06; and 
(e) the details of the cotton export plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The Cotton Advisory Board had 
placed the level of cotton production du ring cotton season  2004-05 at 243 
lakh bales (of 170 Kg. each). The estimated level of cotton production for the 
cotton season 2005-06 is around 250 lakh bales. However, the final 
estimation of cotton production for the cotton season 2005-06 is yet to be 
made. 
With good prospects of cotton crop for the second consecutive season as 
also due to easy availability of cotton, the domestic prices during 2005-06 
season have been subdued. As per the information supplied by the Cotton 
Corporation of India (CCI), the pr ogressive average rate of kapas was 
varying between Rs. 1723/- per quintal and Rs. 1977/- per quintal in different 
States for various varieties as on 12th December, 2005 against the Minimum 
Support Price (MSP) fixed by the Government at Rs. 1760/-and Rs. 1980/- 
per quintal for different staple lengths. 
(c) Exports of cotton in the country were placed under Open General 
Licence (OGL) from 2001 and anybody can export cotton from the country. 
However, looking to the carry over stock from previous year and the crop 
prospects, after meeting the domestic requirements, sufficient quantity may 
be available for exports during the current cotton season. Exports of cotton 
from the country shall however depend upon price parity. 
(d) As per the available reports, due to significant decrease in cotton area 
as also due to heavy rains in China (Main land), the cotton production is 
likely to be affected and as per In ternational Cotton Advisory Committee 
(ICAC) the same is estimated at 5.77 m illion tonnes as against 6.32 million 
tonnes during the previous year. As against this, significantly higher textile 
exports and expanding domestic textile consumption is expected to boost 
cotton use in China (Main land) from 8.2 to 8.6 million tonnes. As per latest 
ICAC release of 1st November, 2005, with projected gap of 2.86 million 
tonnes between production and consumption and with low carry over stocks, 
China (main land) is expected to increase its imports to fill the gap. The 
imports by China are forecast at 2.93 million tonnes as against 1.39 million 
tonnes last season. 
98 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) As already stated above, the exports of cotton are under OGL.

Agreement with manufacturers on drug price control 
2609. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: W ill the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state; 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have not been able to arrive at 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
an agreement with manufacturers to fix prices of life saving and other drugs; 
(b) if so, the areas of disagreement; and 
(c) what steps Government propose to take to ensure availability of life 
saving drugs to patients at reasonable rates? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (c) As per the present Pharma Pricing Policy, the 
74 bulk drugs specified in the First Schedule of the Drugs (Prices Control) 
Order, 1995 (DPCO, 95) and the formulations based thereon are under price 
control and their prices are fixed/re vised by the National Pharmaceutical 
Pricing Authority (NPPA) in accordance with the provisions ofthe DPCO,95. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the various factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc., The NPPA monitors 
the prices of medicines as per monthly Retail Audit Reports of ORG-IMS 
Research Pvt. Ltd. The Government takes corrective measures where the 
public interest is found to be adversely affected. 
Subsequently, a Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, 
Principal Adviser, Planning Commission was constituted to explore options 
other than price control to make ava ilable life saving drugs at reasonable 
prices. During its meetings, the Task Force deliberated upon almost all the 
recommendations made in its interim Report by the Committee under the 
Chairmanship of Joint Secretary. The Ta sk Force has submitted its report to 
the Government on the 20th September, 2005. Some of the salient 
recommendations of Task Force regarding the price management are, that 
Price Controls should be imposed on the 'essentiality' of the drug and not on 
the basis of turnover and it should be applied only to formulations and not to 
bulk drugs, to promote generic drugs, to establish price negotiation process 
for new patented drugs, to streamline the bulk procurement regime, to exempt 
the excise duty, customs duty and other levies on cancer and anti-HIV/AIDS 
drugs, to reduce the excise duty on drugs from 16 to 8% , to enhance the 
exemption limit of SSI units from 
102 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Rs. 1 Crores to Rs. 5 Crores. All these recommendations would assist in 
ensuring that the essential medicines are available at reasonable prices. 
The Government in consultation with various stakeholders is examining 
the recommendations of the Task Force. Based on this a new Pharmaceutical 
Policy is likely to be announced shortly. However, there is no practice of 
having an agreement with manufacturers to fix the prices of life saving and 
other drugs.

According to Indian Council of Medi cal Research, Hepatitis B infection is

diseases, case fatality rate for Japanese Encephalitis and Dengue is 25% and

Diseases provides technical support to the State Governments and undertakes 
surveillance, early detection, prevention and control of outbreaks of 
communicable diseases. The Government of India has launched an integrated 
Disease Surveillance Programme in N ovember 2004 to further strengthen

lodization of salt 
2650. SHRI THENNALA G. BA LAKRISHNA PILL AI: Will the 
Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the WHO has confirmed that even a modest dietary intake of 
iodine by people who are not iodine-deficient will not be harmful but 
beneficial; 
(b) whether Government will consider salt iodization as a public health 
measure and mandate for blanket iodination of salt at salt heads; and 
(c) whether Government have laid down proper packing norms for the 
manufacturers of iodised salt? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) 
According to World Health Organization document No. WHO/NHD/01.1, 
Iodine deficiency disorders are easiest and most cost effective of all disorders 
to prevent. The addition of  a small amount of Iodine to the salt that people 
consume every day is sufficient to prevent Iodine deficiency disorders. 
Consumption of Iodised salt (as per standards laid down under the 
Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954)by people who are not Iodine 
deficient is absolutely safe. 
(b) PFA Rules, 1955 have been amended vide GSR 670(E) dated 
17.11.2005 whereby restrictions have been imposed on the sale of common 
salt for direct human consumption unless the same is iodized. However, 
common salt would continue to be sold for iodization, iron fortification, 
animal use, preservation, manufacturing of medicines and industrial use with 
the prescribed label declaration. 
(c) Packing norms for iodized salt have not been prescribed under PFA 
Rules, 1955. However, as per practice the iodized salt is packed for retail sale 
in polythene packages and for bulk transporation it is packed in bags. The 
iodized salt is not transported in loose conditions. 
To take care of loss of iodine during storage and transportation of iodized 
salt the parameter of iodine content in iodized salt has been prescribed both 
at manufacturer's level at not less than 30 ppm and at retail level at not less 
than 15 ppm.

Diabetic population in India 
2651. SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) The percentage of urban rural population who were suffering from 
diabetes; and

the disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Studies 
until early 1970s essentially showed prevalence rates of diabetes less than 
3%. A study in 1972 showed a prevalence of 2.7% in urban Delhi and 1.9% 
in rural areas near Delhi. More recent studies (1990-2001) show a 
significantly higher prevalence than that above. Studies in southern India 
report an overall prevalence of diabetes of 5%. An additional 2% suffered 
from impaired glucose tolerance. Recen t trends indicate 8-11.8% prevalence 
in urban areas.

health care delivery system in Indi a. Difficult and complicated cases are 
treated at higher centres e.g. Medical Colleges, District Hospitals etc. The 
health education is carried out to make  the public aware diabetics prevention 
and treatment.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (f) The 
World Health Organization have released the World Health Report 2005 in 
which, among another things, they have highlighted the status of the health 
of mothers and children in 192 countries of the world. According to this 
Report, India is among the 51 countries which have shown a slow decline in 
reducing mortality among children under 5 years of age. The Report further 
states that these 51 coun tries will need to accelerat e their efforts over the 
next 10 years for achieving the mille nnium development goals on Infant and 
Maternal Mortality Rates by the year 2015. 
150 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
According to data from the Sample Registration System (SRS) of the 
office of the Registrar General of India (RGI) the Maternal Mortality Ratio 
(MMR) in India was estimated as 407 per 100,000 live births in 1998. 
Subsequent estimates are not available. Based on this data, it is estimated 
that more than 1.1 lakh women die in India every year due to causes related 
to pregnancy and child birth. 
According to the data from SRS of RGI for Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) 
for 2003 is estimated as 60 per 1000 live births. There has been a consistent 
declining trend in infant morality rate over the years. 
The World Health Report does not provide detailed statistics on 
nutritional status of children in India.  However, according to data available 
from the National Family Health Survey-ll (NHFS) conducted in the year 
1998-99, 47% of children under 3 years of age were found to be 
underweight. 
According to estimates by RGI, th e Crude Birth Rate (CBR) of the 
country for 2003 was 24.8 per thousand populations which means that for 
every 1000 population, 24.8 children were born every year. According to 
data from SRS - RGI, 60 out of every 1000 children born in a year die during 
the first year of life (Infant Mortality Rate). Of these deaths, 
27 occur during the first week of life and another 13 occur within the first 
28 days of life (Neonatal Mortality Rate), while the remaining 20 occur 
during the rest of the 11 months of first year of life. As per the SRS data 
released by RGI for the year 2002, 17.8 children out of all the children below 
5 years die every year. All the indicat ors have been showing a declining 
trend over the years. 
The interventions for improving maternal health are essential obstetric 
care, emergency obstetric care, referral  transport for pregnant women with 
complication of pregnancy through Panchayat, provision of drugs and 
equipments at First Referral Units (FRUs), provision of contractual staff like 
additional Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANMs), staff nurses and hiring of 
anesthetists. In the second  phase of theRCH Programme, provision has been 
made to accelerate the decline of Ma ternal Mortality and Morbidity by 
introducing new interventions like Janani Suraksha Yojana operationalization 
of First Referral Units (FRUs), providing 24-hour delivery and new born care 
services at Community Health Centre s (CHCs) and Primary Health Centres 
(PHCs) and training of ANM and LHVto become skill birth attendants.

deficiency and essential new born care. As part of the second phase of RCH 
Programme, the integrated Management for Newborn and Childhood illness 
will be implemented in the districts in a phased manner. 
Government of India ha ve recently launched the National Rural Health

objective of achieving cure rate of 85% of new sputum positive cases and to

by X-ray helps in detecting and curing infectious cases on priority. Facilities

strengthened. Drugs are provided under observation and patients are 
monitored so that they complete their treatment. Drugs are provided free of 
cost in patient-wise boxes. Presently, about 1065 million population in more

AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:

throughout the country for prevention of TB. effectively;

programme;

yet to be covered?

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) 
Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP), widely known as 
DOTS, which is a WHO recommended strategy, with the objective of 
achieving cure rate of 85% of new sputum positive cases and to detect at 
least 70% of such cases, is being implemented in the country since year 1997

this regard is being monitored regularly. It is expected that these districts 
would also be covered under DOTS strategy shortly.

2672.    DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
DR. KARAN SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether international scientific journals recently raised doubts on 
credibility of certain drug research work in India; 
(b) whether his Ministry is taking steps to regulate clinical research. 
(c) if so, whether Government have set up a Central Drug Standard 
Control Organisation under Drug Controller General of India for the 
purpose: 
(d) whether Government have contacted a panel of regulators mostly 
eminent doctors and researchers to inspect  the research sites in their zones; 
and 
(e) if so, to what extent these steps will be helpful to regulate clinical 
research? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (e) 
Certain country specific issues such as  lack of clear regulatory norms and 
intellectual property right issues were earlier considered barriers to global 
clinical research development in India. Now, regulations for conducting 
clinical trials in the country have be en prescribed under Rules-122DA-122E 
& Schedule-Y to the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. 
Good Clinical Practices (GCP), an et hical and scientific quality standard 
for designing and conducting and recording trials data etc. has been 
published in 2001. Ethical guidelines for conducting human trials have also 
been published by Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) in 2000. 
In the past clinical trials in India, pertaining to totally new molecules have 
been very miniscule. However, this trend is now changing and the numbers 
of multicentric global clinical trials in India is expected to increase. 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
CDSCO has, therefore evolved a strategy to start inspections of clinical trial 
centers. 
Number of workshops have already been held in coordination with 
Department of Pharmacology, BYL Nair Hospital, Mumbai along with 
centers at AIIMS, New Delhi, Pondicherry, Kolkata, Hyderabad to develop 
necessary Standard Operating Proceduresm (SOPs), protocols etc. A training 
programme for the prospective inspectors of clinical trials was conducted in 
New Delhi on 20-21 September 2005 with support from WHO and in 
partnership with various medical experts and researchers from pharma 
industry to develop competence and capacity to undertake inspections/ 
audits. 
These measures will significantly enhance standards of clinical trials and 
will address the prevailing perception about likely exploitation of Indian 
study subjects, especially the poor and illiterate.

be tapered off in a span of ten years from now; 
(c) whether steel industry is pitching for a total and immediate ban on iron ore 
exports, while the ore export lobby wants exports to continue indefinitely; and 
(d) whether an abrupt ban on iron ore export would adversely affect the ore mining 
industry in Karnataka and Goa with a lot of investments in ports and mines and the 
machinery would become idle? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) As per 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
provisional figures provided by Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) the production 
of iron ore during 2004-05 was 142.7 million tonnes. IBM has not provided 
any firm estimate of domestic demand of iron ore during the same period. 
However, based on crude steel production during 2004-05, the domestic 
consumption of iron ore is estimated to be in excess of 54 million tonnes. 
(b) Exports of iron ore did not form a part of the terms of reference of the 
"Expert Group" which was constituted by the Ministry of Steel under the 
Chairmanship of Shri R.K. Dang as  hence no specific recommendation has 
been made in the report of the "Expert Group" for tapering off iron ore 
exports in a span of ten years from now. However, Shri R.K. Dang has 
separately submitted a list titled "Oth er observations and recommendations" 
covering areas outside the terms of re ference of the "Exp ert Group". This, 
inter alia, contains recommendations for stopping exports of high and 
medium grade lump iron ore (except if being sold under existing long term 
international contracts of NMDC); phasing out exports of high grade iron ore 
fines and canalization of exports, within ceilings, of medium grade iron ore 
fines. 
(c) Some steel producers and associations representing various sections of 
the steel industry have represented for placing curbs on export of iron ore. On 
the other hand, represented against any move for placing curbs or ban on 
exports of iron ore. 
(d) The iron ore produced in  Karnataka and Goa is predominantly medium 
and low grade. Besides production of fines is predominant in these states. The 
domestic and local demand for such ore is low, on account of inadequate 
agglomeration and benefication capacities in the country and limited local 
steel making capacities in these states. As such production in these states is 
primarily dependent on the export market and an abrupt ban on exports of iron 
ore can be expected to affect production of iron ore in these states. This could 
also have a consequential impact on utilization of investments in both ports 
and the mines.
