PRIVATE MEMBER'S RESOLUTION Need to ameliorate economic 
condition of farmers in the backdrop of natural 
calamities 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY(Pondicherry):   Sir, I move the following 
Resolution- 
"Having regard to the fact that - 
(i) even after more than five decades of independence the overall lot of 
farmers, who constitute majority of  the population of the nation, has 
not improved to the desired level and it is indeed very sad that 
thousands of farmers have committed suicide during the last few 
years, unable to face the miseries and hardships by themselves and 
their families and due to the pressure on them to repay their loans 
taken from moneylenders, banks, cooperatives, etc.; 
(ii) majority of the farmers are inde bted in the country because they do 
not get remunerative prices of thei r produce mostly due to the faulty 
procurement policy of the Govern ment and the nexus between the 
private traders and the Governme nt procurement agencies which 
forces them to sell their produce at throwaway prices; 
(iii) the farmers face the brunt of natural calamities such as drought, flood 
and their crops, dwelling units, household items including food   
grains,   livestock    are   affected   and    their   miseries   are 
250 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
compounded     due    to   non   extension   of   compulsory   crop 
insurance to their crops and livestock; 
(iv) whenever the farmers grow bumper  crops the prices of the produces 
nosedive in the market and by the time Market Intervention is 
introduced all is over for the farmers; and 
(v)   Governments while formulating the Plans and incentives have not 
given adequate attention to the pl ight of farmers and that only a 
meagre  percentage of GDP has so far  been  allocated for the 
agriculture. 
this House urges upon the Government to - 
(a) announce a package for the farmers who are indebted or 
adversely affected, by natural calamity through waiver of loans, 
interest accrued on loans and by providing fresh loans to start 
agricultural operations and such other measures as the 
Government may deem necessary; 
(b) plug the loopholes in the procurement policy and give the 
minimum support price to the farmers without any hassles; 
(c) insure the farmers and their crops and livestock at a nominal 
premium or at   the Government   cost compulsorily; 
(d) allocate appropriate percentage of GDP to agriculture; 
(e) make Market    Intervention   compulsory   whenever   there    
is bumper  crop of any commodity; and 
(f) take such other measures for the welfare of farmers as the 
Government may deem necessary. 
Sir, this is a very important Resolution and aims at improving the 
life of our farmers in various fields, especially through adequate credit facilities 
for them, marketing support for their produce, strengthening  of cooperative 
institutions, enabling farmers to use the latest advancements of science and 
technology in the farm sector, insuring farmers produce, etc. These are the 
areas which I what the Government to consider seriously. 
Therefore, before going into the points one-by-one, I would like to 
request the Government to announce a package for the farmers who are 
indebted or adversely affected by natural calamity through waiver of loans, 
interest accrued on loans and by providing fresh loans to start agriculture 
251 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
operations and such other measures  as the Government may deem 
necessary; to plug the loopholes in the procurement policy and give the 
minimum support price to the farmers wi thout any hassles; insure the farmers 
and their crops and livestock at a nominal premium or at the Government cost 
compulsorily; allocate appropriate perc entage of GDP to agriculture; make 
market intervention compulsory whe never there is bumper crop of any 
commodity; and take such other measures for the welfare of farmers as the 
Government may deem necessary. 
Sir, we find that in spite of  the support given by the State 
Governments and the Central Government, today, the farmers are, at a loss, 
because they are having small holdings and agricultural operations have 
become very costly. We find that a farmer is holding two acres of land or three 
acres of land to start cultivation a nd invest money on seeds, fertilisers, 
irrigation and electricity. When the harve st comes, the farmers are, at a loss, 
because they are not getting the minimum support price for their produce. The 
reason is, when there is a bumper crop, the intermediaries and traders get 
more profit by purchasing the farmer's produce at a distress price On the other 
hand, even when they take their produc e to the cooperative marketing area, 
or, in the State Marketing Committees, th ey take only a limited quantity, and 
the support that is being given through market intervention is not sufficient for 
the farmers. As a result, there is a lot of migration from agriculture to other 
areas. The farmers are leaving their cultivation and coming to urban areas for 
earning their livelihood. 
Sir, as per the report of the Samp le Survey Organisation, there are 
about 660 million marginal farmers. About 40 per cent of them want to leave 
cultivation because they are not .getti ng profit or even the minimum support 
price for their produce. This is the finding of the Sample Survey Organisation. 
As a result, farmers are not attracted towards agriculture. 
Sir, I am very happy that the UPA Government under Dr. Manmohan 
Singh's leadership is doing many things for the farmers. The Finance Minister 
has announced loans worth Rs.1,10,000 Crores from the nationalised banks, 
the scheduled banks and cooperative in stitutions to the farmers for the 
purpose of cultivation. Sir, I had also  put a question to the hon. Finance 
Minister that, last year, out of the to tal allocation of Rs.95,000 Crores, more 
than 80 per cent of that money was not distributed to the farmers-. This year, it 
has been increased to Rs.1.10 Crores. I told the Finance Minister to have a 
Committee at the State level and at the district level to monitor the situation, it 
should see to it that the money which has 
252 

[16 December,. 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
been earmarked for giving loan to the farmers for agricultural purposes is 
properly distributed by the various scheduled banks and the nationalised 
banks. But, unfortunately, the hon. Fi nance Minister said that he was 
reviewing it. 
Sir, as far as the nationalised banks, scheduled banks and the 
cooperative banks are concerned, they do not extend loans to the poor 
farmers. When we take the farmers to these banks, we also get negative 
replies. This is the attitude of these banks towards these poor farmers. Even a 
small and marginal farmer is mainly depending- upon the loan which is made 
available to him through the nationalised banks and the scheduled banks. 
Why are the farmers committing suicides whether it is Andhra 
Pradesh or whether it is Karnataka or whether it is Maharashtra or whether it is 
Orissa or any other State? I am not going into the politics. Farmers are 
committing suicide because of indebtedness. Indebtedness is the . major 
cause. They are not able to get t he loan from the banking institutions, 
therefore, they approach t he moneylenders, the organised gangs in the rural 
areas who charge more than four times of the interest that is generally charged 
by the banks. What happens is that the farmers are indebted and when their 
crop fails they are not able to pay back the loan and they go to the extent of 
committing suicide. Their families are in distress. This is a very serious matter. 
During last Session also, we discussed the same subject in this august House. 
With regard to the Crop Insurance Act, the State Government and the Central 
Government should take steps. Crop insurance is a solution, which will 
definitely help the farming community as  a whole. Take the case of floods, 
which are there in several parts of the country. Then, we have drought in some 
parts of the country. We find that t he farmers are at loss. When there are 
floods, the entire crop is damaged. Only a few big farmers insure their crops. 
The marginal and small farmers are not able to insure their crops. When they 
get loan from the banks sometimes they insure the crops of the farmers. Some 
of them are not doing that too. Sir, it is  high time that we took care of it. The 
hon. Prime Minister when he was the Finance Minister announced several 
times that there should be a universal insurance scheme for the farmers in this 
country. That has to be worked out because sometimes it may be a feasible 
proposition and sometimes insurance companies may not agree. But there 
should a workable solution. Chief Minister s of all the States have to be called, 
there should be a discussion, a final solution can be arrived at

as to how farmers' crops can be insured, and livestock can be insured. Today 
with a very small income the farmer has to sustain his.family. He has to 
educate his children and thereafter he has to perform functions in his family. 
With the meagre income that he is getting from the agricultural land, it is very 
difficult for him to do all these things. Therefore, Sir, the crop insurance is a 
must in order to bring them out of debt  trap as far as farmers are concerned.

OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to 
the passing away of Shri P.M. Sayeed , a Member of this House, on the 18 th 
December, 2005, at Seoul following cardiac arrest.   He was 65 years of age. 
Born at Androth Island, Lakshadweep, in May, 1941, Shri Sayeed 
had his education at the Government Arts College, Mangalore and Sidhartha 
College of Law, Mumbai. 
A lawyer, a political and social worker, Shri Sayeed devoted his life 
for the welfare of the poor and the downtrodden. He was associated with 
various social, welfare and cultural activ ities, particularly in Lakshadweep; 
and was instrumental in conducting inter-State cultural programmes and 
promoting folk arts of Lakshadweep. 
Shri Sayeed had a long and illustrious political career, which started 
with the membership of the Fourth L ok Sabha. He had the distinction of 
winning the Lok Sabha Election for ten times consecutively. He also served as 
Deputy Speaker of the Twelfth Lok Sa bha and the Thirteen th Lok Sabha. He 
was also Member of the Panel of Chairmen, Lok Sabha, from 1991 to 1992 
and 1996 to 1997. 
Shri Sayeed also served as the Un ion Minister of State and held the 
portfolios of Steel, Coal and Mines from 1979 to 1980; Home Affairs from 
1993 to 1995 and Information and Broadcasting from 1995 to 1996 and Union 
Minister of Power from May, 2004 till he breathed his last. 
Shri Sayeed was Chairman of  the Committee on Provision of 
Computers to Members of Parliamen t; Committee on Private Members' Bills 
and Resolutions, Lok Sabha; Committee on Budget of Lok Sabha; Library 
Committee and Joint Parliamentary Committee on Security Matters in 
Parliament Complex. He was also Secr etary and Deputy Chief Whip of the 
Congress Parliamentary Party. 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2005]  
Shri Sayeed represented the National Capital Territory of Delhi in 
this House from August, 2004 till date. 
A widely travelled person, Shri Sayeed visited many countries as a 
Member and Leader of various Parliamentary delegations. 
Shri Sayeed was a soft-spoken person and was highly respected. He 
endeared himself to one and all with his suave manners. 
In the passing away of Shri P.M. Sayeed, the country has lost an 
eminent Parliamentarian and an able administrator. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri P.M. Sayeed. 
I request Members to rise in thei r places and observe silence as a 
mark of respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members 
of the bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy. 
As a mark of respect in the memory of Shri Sayeed, a sitting 
Member, the House stands adjourned till 11.00 a.m. on Tuesday, the 2oth 
December, 2005. 
The House then adjourned at five minutes past eleven of the clock  
till eleven of the clock on Tuesday, the 20lh December, 2005.

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
New Opium Policy 
The licensing conditions for grant of opium cultivation have a clause on 
forewarning the farmers about the conditions for licence in the next crop year. 
Among the clauses of forewarning issued in the Licensing Conditions last year 
(for the crop year 2004-05), there was a stipulation that "cultivators who had 
tendered opium during the crop year 2004-05 which has been found to be of a 
consistency lower than 55 degree will be debarred from licence for the crop year 
2005-06." This forewarning clause has been incorporated into the opium policy 
for the current crop year 2005-06 
The clause has been introduced in view of the growing tendency of 
cultivators of tendering water mixed opium. Under this provision, those 
cultivators who tender opium of consistency lower than 55 degree have not been 
issued licence during the crop year 2005-06. 3767 out of 72480

It has been observed that during the past few years there has been an increasing 
trend in tendering 'water mixed' opium. The 'water mixed' opium is being tendered 
by some unscrupulous cultivators deliberately to substitute for the raw opium 
apparently diverted to illicit channels for manufacture of heroin in illicit, 
make-shift laboratories. It was, therefore, felt necessary to debar such 
cultivators from opium cultivation. The government benefits by ge tting better 
quality opium by curbing the tendency of cultivators to mix water with opium and 
by controlling possible diversion of the narcotic material.

Loans to SSIs and agricultural sectors by public sector banks 
t*386. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the measures taken by Government to provide loans to small scale 
industries and agricultural sectors through public sector banks at cheap rate of 
interest; 
(b) what is the percentage of rate of interest at which loans to these sectors 
are provided currently; 
(c) what are the terms and conditions and time limit for loans without 
security; and 
(d) details of loans sanctioned to small scale industrial units by banks during 
the past three years, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM); (a) and (b) A 
policy was announced in June, 2004 envisaging doubling the flow of credit to 
agriculture from 2004-05 to 2006-07. Government has also announced a 
Policy Package which envisages doubling of credit flow from the public sector 
banks to the small and medium enterprises sector over the five years starting 
2005-06. This policy would provide adequate enhancement of credit to SME 
sector. 
As per the interest rate policy of Reserve Bank of India (RBI), interest rates 
on loans given by commercial banks have been deregulated. However, the interest rate 
on loans up to Rs. 2 lakh should not exceed the Benchmark Prime Lending Rate 
(BPLR) of the banks concerned. BPLR is fixed taking into account inter-alia, 
their cost of funds, transaction cost and risk cost. Hence, the rate of interest on 
loans upto Rs. 2 lakhs is the barest minimum.

Stamp duty on green market transactions 
*390. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI. Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have received representation from the 
Association of National Stock Exchange Members of India (ANSEMI) stating that 
equal investors have to pay stamp duty twice on all green market transactions 
routed through terminals located outside Maharashtra; 
(b) if so, the details of other issues raised therein; 
(c) whether any intervention of his Ministry has prompted the State 
Government of Maharashtra to revise its earlier decision; 
(d) whether Government are aware that Maharashtra Government has decided 
to revise its earlier decision in this regard; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (e) Under the 
Constitution of India, Stamp Duties (but not including rates of stamp duty) falls under 
Entry 44 of the Concurrent List. The Central Government has powers to fix the rates 
of stamp duty in respect of 10 instruments specified in Entry 91 of the Union List, 
whereas States have the powers in respect of the remaining instruments by virtue of Entry 63 
of the State List. The revenue from stamp duty is collected and appropriated by the 
State in which it is leviable. The Indian Stamp Act, 1899, lays down the law 
relating to Stamps. 
The Government of Maharashtra made an amendment in the Bombay Stamp Act, 1958, 
through the Bombay Stamp (Amendment) Ordinance, 2005 (which has since been 
replaced by an Act of State Legislature), inter-alia, inserting Article 51A which provides 
that record of transactions (electronic or otherwise) effected by a trading member referred to in 
section 10B, shall be subject to rates of stamp duty specified in this Article. The effect of 
this amendment is that records of all transactions carried out in stock exchanges located 
in Maharashtra (like BSE and NSE) shall be subjected to stamp duty in Maharashtra, 
irrespective of where the brokers or the investors are looted. 
The Association of National Stock Exchange Members of India (ANMI) had made a 
representation to the Government of India, inter-alia, stating that the amendment made by 
"Government of Maharashtra amounts to extra-territorial application of law since NSE 
members are located in every State of India, that the provisions of Article 51A are 
ambiguous in the sense that they do not clearly specify as to which instrument or record of 
transactions (out of a number of records created during transactions) shall be liable to stamp 
duty, and also that it tries to circumvent the Central laws and seeks to levy a Security 
Transaction Tax, in the garb of stamp duty. 
The Government of India, Ministry of Finance, had taken up the matter with the 
Government of Maharashtra, requesting them to reconsider their decision, as the amendment 
made by the State Government may lead to inter-state jurisdictional disputes, lead to 
avoidable litigation, and adversely affect the national character of stock exchanges, 
thereby hampering development of capital market in the country. The Government 
of Maharashtra has informed that the matter is under their consideration and that the final 
decision is not yet taken. 
40 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
A writ petition has been filed before the Hon'ble Delhi High Court 
challenging the validity of the amendment.

affected both banks and their clients;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) to (c) World Bank has brought out a report in 
December 2004 titled "Scaling up Access to Finance for India's Rural Poor". 
Certain observations have been made in the report regarding functioning of rural 
financial institutions in India including problems faced by rural poor relating to 
absence of flexible products & services, high transaction costs, insistence on 
collaterals and interest rate restrictions. Certain suggestions have been made 
including providing flexible products at competitive prices to rural poor, need for 
composite financial services, simplification of banking procedures, better staffing 
policies and door step banking, use of technology etc. Further, it has been 
suggested to revisit the policies on setting caps on interest rate on deposits and 
advances, priority sector lending, restructuring the RRBs and Rural Cooperative 
Banks, better regulation and supervision and active role of Government in facilitating 
rural finance markets. 
(d) and (e) Government and RBI constantly monitor the credit needs of 
different sectors of the economy and undertake corrective measures, whenever 
required, to ensure that adequate funds flow to Agriculture, Small & Medium 
Enterprises and such other important sectors. RBI has already

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) to (c) Government has decided, in principle, to

There are a number of large, profitable, unlisted CPSEs, which would gain

opportunity to investors to invest in these CPSEs. It also provides greater 
liquidity for the trading of these CPSE shares. Employees of the CPSEs would 
also get an opportunity for investing in these shares through reservation of a 
part of the offered shares for subscription by them.

of a small proportion of the Government's shareholding in CPSEs would be 
channelised into the National Investment Fund.

Subjects transferred to Panchayats 
t2976. SHRIMATI SUSHMA SW ARAJ: Will the Minister of 
PANCHAYATI RAJ be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that under 73rd and 74th amendments of the Constitution, 23 
main subjects were to be transferred to the Panchayats; 
(b) if so, the names of the States in which these subjects have been transferred; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Central Government to get these subjects transferred to 
Panchayats in the States where the same have not been transferred as yet? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): 
(a) Article 243G of the Constitution (73rd Amendment) Act, 1992 provides that the State 
Legislature may devolve powers and responsibilities upon Panchayats with respect to the 
implementation of Schemes for economic development and social justice as may be 
entrusted to them including those in relation to the matters listed in the Eleventh Schedule. 
This Schedule lists 29 matters. 
(b) and (c) As the Constitution provides that it is legislatures of States that will 
endow the Panchayati Raj Institutions with powers and authority, all the States 
covered by the 73rd Amendment Act, have devolved matters to them in varying 
measure. Effective devolution of functions would need to be accompanied by 
devolution of funds and functionaries to the Panchayati Raj Institutions in order to 
empower them to function as institutions of self government in accordance with the 
Constitutional mandate. In order to evolve a national consensus on the measures to be 
taken to strengthen Panchayati Raj and ensure that Panchayati Raj Institutions function 
as institutions of self-government as envisaged in Part IX of the Constitution, the 
Ministry of Panchayati 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
135 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
Raj convened Seven Round Tables of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj between July, 
2004 and December, 2004. At the Round Tables, about 150 points for action, covering 
18 dimensions of Panchayati Raj, were formulated by consensus, inter-alia, these 
cover points of action pertaining to both the Centre and the States, relating to the 
effective devolution of functions, funds and functionaries to Panchayats. At the Kolkata 
Round Table, it was agreed that while devolution must eventually comprise the entire range 
of subjects provided for in the State legislation in a time-bound manner, States may prioritize 
their devolution programme to ensure that for such functions as are prioritized, there is 
full and effective devolution in empowering PRIs as institutions of self-government in 
respect of these functions. To this end, the first step is identification of activities related 
to devolved functions for each tier of Panchayati Raj Institutions within a time-bound 
period. The next step should be the devolution of functionaries to the Panchayati Raj 
Institutions on the basis of the activities to be performed at each tier. The final step which 
would complete the cycle of devolution wlould consist in the devolution of finances 
commensurate with the activities to be performed at each level of the Panchayati Raj 
Institutions. 
A Council of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj under the Chairmanship of the Union 
Minister for Panchayati Raj has been constituted to review the implementation of the 
recommendations. The first meeting of the Council was held on 5th-6th August, 2005 at 
Kochi, Kerala. A Committee of Chief Secretaries of States and State Panchayati Raj 
Secretaries has also been constituted under the Chairmanship of the Union Secretary 
(Panchayati Raj) to monitor the progress on the implementation of the 150 
recommendations of the Seven Round Tables and the decisions of the Council of State 
Ministers of Panchayati Raj. Four review meetings of the Committee have so far been held in 
April, 2005, June, 2005, September, 2005, and November 2005. 
With a view to interacting with Panchayats and carrying out a review with the 
authorities concerned of the progress in implementing the points for action mutually 
agreed to in the Round Tables, a process of visiting the States and UTs at the level 
of Union Minister for Panchayati Raj has been initiated. Eight States have been 
covered so far. These include Karnataka, West Bengal, Uttaranchal, Haryana, 
Chhattisgarh, Orissa, Arunachal Pradesh and Rajasthan. Each visit is 
136

concluded with a Statement of Conclusions jointly signed with the Chief 
Minister of the State concerned, laying out the points of action on which the 
State would move to operationalise the recommendations of the Round Tables.

Confederation of Indian Industries (CII) are working together to facilitate building 
linkages between Panchayats, Industries and business to create Rural Business Hubs 
(RBH) in different blocks of the country on the lines of the successful Thai 
experience of One Tambon One Product (OTOP). Rural Business Hubs will be a 
Public-Private-Panchayat Partnership to produce/improve/refine goods from 
locally available resources to enable larger market access. A joint RBH Council, 
comprising representatives of the Government and CII and eminent individuals 
working in this area, has been constituted for monitoring the process and reviewing 
the actions. 
At the initial phase, only one product from one Block Panchayat of all the 
States will be selected for setting up of  RBH. The State Governments with the 
help of Panchayats and Cll will identify the potential product which will be promoted 
covering every facet starting from product development to sales, with the focus on 
creating value addition and securing better prices. In the 'second stage, a Task 
Force of key stakeholders and resource personnel will be set up for ensuring 
development of the RBH in a set time frame. The Task Force will envaluate the product 
and prepare strategy for ensuring quality, better pricing and market access. 
(c) This initiative of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj was initially limited to 
nine states, to start with, as the newly formed Ministry of Panchayati Raj was 
taking shape and there was a shortage of officers and staff to follow up. These 
States were selected on the basis of initial response and interest shown by the 
states. The initiative has since been extended to all States/UTs covered by Part 
IX of the Constitution. 
(d) and (e) The financing of Rural Business Hubs is envisaged as a business 
proposition on the public-private-panchayat-partnership principle which will be supported by 
such 'top-up' funds as may be available for the purpose. Assistance is also envisaged 
from specialized institutions like NABARD, SIDBI, the Institution of Engineers in 
the form of finance, professional and technical guidance to panchayats for identifying 
and setting up RBHs. 
(f) The process of setting up of RBHs has already begun with the signing of 
three Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) in the States of

Uttaranchal and Haryana. The first MOU under the RBH initiative was signed in 
Dehra Dun (Uttaranchal) for setting up a rural business hub for processing fruit grown in 
the Ramgarh block and few other Blocks of Nainital District. Thereafter, three more 
MOUs have been finalized and signed to set up RBHs for Jatropha plantation and 
production of bio-diesel in Faridabad and Mewat Districts of Haryana and Dungarpur 
District of Rajasthan. Subsequent to  an advertisement in certain leading 
newspapers, over 150 responses have been received from Panchayati Raj Institutions 
(PRIs) and individuals. A conclave of all the stakeholders involved in the development of 
bio-diesel from Jatropha, through Panchayats under the RBH initiative of the Ministry, was 
held on 5th November, 2005. In this conclave, which was attended by 100 PRI 
representatives from all over the country, it was decided to set up a joint committee of the 
Ministry of Panchayati Raj, Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas and Planning 
Commission alongwith the stakeholders including scientists and other corporate, for the 
development of Bio-Fuels through Panchayats under the RBH initiative. The RBH 
initiative is also scheduled to be discussed in the next meeting of the Council of States 
Ministers on Panchayati Raj.

Feasibility study on coal gasification 
2983. SHRI CHITTABRATA MAJUMDAR: SHRI 
DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether GAIL has initiated action for commissioning a detailed feasibility 
report study for commercial implementation of coal gasification process; 
(b) if so, the status of the report;

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. GAIL (India) Limited (GAIL) are 
carrying out a detailed feasibility study for a coal gasification project. 
GAIL have opted for the Shell coal gasification process and have 
commissioned UHDE India Limited to carry out the feasibility study with 
Shell technology.  
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. (ONGC) have signed a 
Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the National Mining Research Centre, 
Skochinsky Institute of Mining (NMRC-SIM), Moscow, Russia for consultancy for an 
Underground Coal Gasification (UCG) project. The total agreed program of work for the 
UCG project will comprise six phases covering site selection, detailed evaluation of 
geological and hydroiogical data, preparation of the technical report, project design, 
construction of enterprise UCG, and its implementation. The planned duration of the 
project is 60 months. The total financial implication is US$ 15.32 million. In the first 
phase of the agreement, data of some coal fields will be analysed for identifying a 
suitable site for pilot testing the UCG process in shallow coals to start with.

Statement 
ROUND TABLE OF ASIAN OIL MINISTERS 
SUMMARY OF CONCLUSIONS 
NEW DELHI, 25 NOVEMBER 2005 
Ministers and Heads of Delegation from the principal Asian oil and gas 
producing countries - the Russian Fe deration, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, 
Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan - met with the principal Asian oil and gas consuming 
countries - Japan, the Republic of Korea, China, Turkey and India at the invitation of His 
Excellency Shri mani Shankar Aiyar, Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas, India, in 
New Delhi on 25 November 2005. 
Noting the conclusions of the January Round Table which had brought together the 
principal West Asian and South-east Asian producing countries with principal Asian 
consuming countries, participants in the November Round Table came to the following 
broad conclusions: 
(i) It was noted that Asia in the 21st century is emerging as the largest single 
supplier of oil and gas, as well as the fastest growing consumption centres in 
the world. 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
(ii) Regional cooperation in the Asian oil and gas economy must be pursued within 
the framework of global cooperation. In this context, they welcomed the 
forthcoming assumption by the co-chair of the Round Table, Russia, of the 
chairmanship of G-8, and expressed the hope that the concerns and views 
expressed in this Round Table would be factored into G-8 initiatives for Energy, 
Ecology and efficiency which Russia proposes to undertake. They also welcomed 
the Russian intention to associate important producers and import-intensive 
countries, including participants in the Round Table, in the deliberations of the 
expert groups that are expected to be set up by G-8. 
(iii) Participants noted with concern the recent volatility in international oil and gas 
prices and agreed that stable and reasonable prices would be in the interests of 
producers and consumers alike to ensure, on the one hand, that the growth 
prospects of consuming countries are not damaged and, on the other, that 
investment in producing countries is promoted. 
(iv) The need was recognised to study the possibility and feasibility of promoting 
and developing gas and oil interconnections through LNG and through trans-
national oil & gas pipelines within the Asian region for integrating energy 
markets, as well as improving the transportation infrastructure, In relation to 
the oil logistics, the Republic of Korea offered to make available crude and product 
storages. This too would be studied. This study could include the 
exploration of all alternative linkages by land and sea throughout Asia, 
including alternatives of linking the Caspian basin to countries in South Asia. 
To this end, the Indian proposal to initiate such a study, in association with 
participating countries, in particular the Republic of Korea which has proposed a 
working group to prepare a master plan, under the overall aegis of the 
International Energy Forum, was endorsed. The study will also take into 
account the suggestion made in one of the presentations to the Round Table of the 
possibility of establishing the proposed Asian Gas Grid Institute. 
152 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
mi) The Japanese proposal was endorsed to study the possibility of     
networking the countries of Central, South and East Asia and 
elsewhere with the Japanese initiative to promote a Sustainable 
and Flexible Energy System (SAFE). 
(vi) The importance of mutual cross-investment to reinforce mutual trade 
in oil and gas and associated downstream industry was emphasized 
as the optimal means of promoting stability, security and sustainability 
in the Asian oil and gas economy. It was emphasized that 
environment-friendly investment in upstream and downstream projects 
should be encouraged, that the investment climate should be improved 
to augment investment in the Asian oil and gas sector, and that Asian 
investment in Asian properties, including those in the Caspian region, 
be supported. Initiatives towards this end were welcomed. 
(vii) The significance of  transparency in access to all relevant data 
relating to reserves, demand, supply and investment was recognized, 
and the importance of predictability was emphasized as a key element 
of stability, security and sustainability in the Asian oil and gas 
economy, and, indeed, the world over. 
(viii) It was agreed that practical steps be taken bilaterally and regionally, 
as well as globally, for networking the knowledge-base of participating 
countries in the development of the Asian oil and gas sector and the 
energy economy in general In this context, the need to move towards 
the most optimal energy mix for each country and towards new and 
renewable energy sources was recognised as a priority for the Asian 
and global economy. 
(ix) It was further agreed that cooperation among participants in human 
resource development and training programmes would contribute an 
important element to the development of the Asian oil and gas economy.

of non-supply of gas despite Centre's commitment in the past; 
(b) whether Government would allocate the required quantity of gas for this project 
from Tapti fields since the production has now started in this field; and 
(c) whether the Central Government has gone back on its commitment leading to grave 
injustice to the Saurashtra region for whose development, this power is very crucial? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYER): (a) to (c) An in-principle allocation of 2.25 MMSCMD of gas was 
made to the Pipavav Power Proejct on the 5th June 2000. This allocation was subject 
to the condition that the Management Committee (MC) of the Tapti field will take 
the investment decision for additional development of the field. It was also stipulated that 
the date of commencement of gas supply could undergo a change depending on the 
investment decision which was to be taken by the MC of the Tapti field. The 'in-
principle' allocation was not a commitment as such but an expressive of the positive 
intent of the Government. It may be mentioned that gas from Additional Development of 
Tapti fields is not covered under the Administered Pricing Mechanism (APM) and the

168

to market JV gas, including additional gas, at market related prices. 
Therefore, the Pipavav Project developers has to tie-up their gas requirement 
with the JV concerned at market-related price. 
Since the allocation for the Pipavav Power Project was tied up with the 
Tapti Field, and the price of gas that would be available after additional 
development of the field is governed by the PSC signed between the operator 
and the Government, the Government of Gujarat have been advised by the 
Central Government to directly approach the Tapti JV for a gas tie-up for the 
proposed project at a mutually negotiated price.

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) LPG requirements are met by a combination of 
domestic production and imports. A temporary shortage of LPG emerged in September

Ltd. (RIL) 
170 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
production was 190 TMT less than planned. In consequence, physical inventories with 
oil marketing companies (OMCs) declined from 333 TMT at the beginning of April,

Catalytic Cracker (FCC) unit at Jamnagar for maintenance work. Moreover, at just 
about the same time, as RIL confirmed its shutdown effective October, 2005, domestic 
production prospects were seriously impacted by the fire in Mumbai High North and 
global LPG supplies became tight, largely on account of the impact of Hurricane 
Katrina on US refineries. All these factors put together upset the plans made by OMCs

composite task force of the OMCs under the close supervision of the Government, 
efforts have been made to overcome the physical shortages of supply. In addition to the 
arrangements made earlier by OMCs to import 642 TMT of LPG during the period October-

TMT during this period. The overall physical shortage in the country at present has been 
reduced to only about 1.5% of the average monthly consumption of LPG. However, the 
backlog at the micro-level may vary from market to market on account of operational 
reasons.

country is just 200 cubic metre per capita at present;

scarcity of water in the country is mounting? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) and (b) There is large temporal 
variation in the rainfall and about 75% of the rainfall occurs during the monsoon

period.

Meter (BCM). Therefore, the per capita storage capacity is 207 cubic metre. 
(e) In view of large temporal variation in availability of water resources, it is necessary 
to conserve the water and create more storage capacity for meeting the future 
requirements.

Cleaning of Rivers and Lakes 
3039. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PI LANIA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that due to siltification, big rivers, lakes, 
dam reservoirs get chocked, which results in loss of water as well as floods; 
(b) if so, what is the estimate of Government regarding the quantum of loss 
per year; 
(c) whether Government have identified certain rivers/reservoirs/lakes etc. 
for desiltification; 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the schemes proposed to be 
undertaken; and 
(e) what steps Government propose to take to improve the scenario 
and to make it labour friendly? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) and (b) As per the 
report namely "Compendium on Silting of Reservoirs in the country (2001)" for 144 
reservoirs, the weighted average annual loss in grass storage due to desiltation has 
been found to be 0.44%. In addition, as per the report of the Multidisciplinary 
Committee (2002) constituted by the Ministry of Water Resources under the 
Chairmanship of Dr. B.K. Mrttal, former Chairman, Central Water Commission, 
siltation in rivers is not pronounced and alarming. The Third Minor Irrigation 
Census (2000-01) has mentioned that about 85,000 tanks and other storages 
are not in use predominantly due to siltation and other factors like lack of 
maintenance, encroachment, etc. 
211 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
(c) to (e) Following the report of Dr. Mittal Committee, the Ministry of 
Water Resources constituted a Select Group under the Chairmanship of 
Chairman, Central Water Commission in order to identify action points in this 
regard. The action points inter alia included identificaion of vulnerable reaches 
along rivers by State Government have subsequently been forwarded to the 
State Governments to take necessary action in this regard. Govt. of India has 
also approved a pilot scheme "National Project for Repair, Renovation and 
Restoration of Water Bodies Directly Linked to Agriculture" in 2004-05 for a 
sanctioned outlay of Rs. 300 Crores to be implemented during the remaining 
period of the X Five Year Plan. The obj ectives of the scheme are to restore 
the storage capacity and the irrigation potential of the water bodies. 
The Central Water Commission has published a study report on siltation 
of reservoirs in January 2001 under the title "Compendium on s ilting of 
reservoirs in India". The report has addressed the issue of siltation of reservoirs and 
desiltation measures including dredging operations etc. It has been concluded 
that a better alternative is to increase the storage capacity of reservoirs in due 
consideration of the sediment loads providing arrangements for flushing of silt in 
the design of the dam and its operation schedule, in case of the new ones and 
raising of the dams whether it is technically feasible.

*378.SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (d) there is no concept like 'One Nation-One 
Education' in the National policy on Education. Education is in the 
Concurrent List and the State Governments are free to devise their 
approaches and plans for Education. It is expected that all their initiatives will be 
within the framework of National Policy on Education. The National policy on 
Education, 1986, as modified in 1992, envisaged a National System of

comparable quality. The National System of Education envisages a common 
educational structure. The 10+2+3 st ructure has now been accepted in all 
parts of the country. The National System of Education also envisages a 
national curricula framework which contains a common core along with other 
components that are flexible.

agencies set up by various Ministri es. These agencies ensure uniform 
recognition of credentials and also quality.

(b) to (d) Land and its management fall within the administrative 
jurisdiction of the respective States as provided under Entry No. 18 of State 
List (List II) of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. The Central 
Government plays only a coordinating and advisory role in this regard. There 
is no Central Law on restoration of alienated tribal land. However, States with

providing for restoration of alienated land. As per reports received from the 
States, 3.75 lakh cases were filed in various Courts comprising an area of 3.46 
lakh hectares, out of which 1.62 lakh cases were decided in favour of tribals and 
1.80 lakh hectares of alienated land have been restored to Schedueld Tribe 
persons. Cases covering 0.58 lakh hectares of land are still pending for disposal 
in various Courts. Data regarding State-wise number of tribals who have been 
deprived of their land in the State are not maintained in the Ministry. 
During 1999-2000, the Ministry of Rural Development had constituted an 
Expert Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri B.N. Yugandhar, IAS 
(Retd.), former Secretary (Rural Development) to look into the existing 
laws/regulations of alienation of tribal lands in the country and to draft a model 
law on the subject in consultation of tribal lands in the country and 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
to draft a model law on the subject in consultation with the States, National 
Commission for Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribes, Ministry of Welfare, etc. 
The Expert Committee has submitted a report, which contains 
recommendations relating to (i) Land and Rights of Scheduled Tribes, (ii) 
Legal Improvements for Enforcement of Land Rights, (iii) Model 
Legislation, (iv) Land Acquisition, Displacement and Rehabilitation, (v) 
Forest Rights of Scheduled Tribes, (vi) Administrative and Organisational 
Measures for Effective Implementation,  and (vii) Socio-Economic Measures. 
Copies of the Report have been sent to the State Governments and to concerned 
Central Ministries for necessary action. However, since land is a State subject, the 
responsibility of enacting necessary legislation as well as ensuring its 
implementation rests with the State Governments. 
The tenurial and access rights of forest dwelling scheduled tribes in respect 
of forest land which they have been traditionally inhabiting for ages have not 
been adequately recognised so far, resulting in historical injustice to them. In 
order to provide a legislative frame-work for recognition of forest rights of the 
forest dwelling Scheduled tribes, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs has introduced 
a "Scheduled Tribes (Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill, 2005" in Lok Sabha on 
13.12.2005. The Bill, when enacted, proposes to recognise the forest rights of 
the forest dwelling scheduled tribes including tenurial security, ownership of 
MFP and certain other rights.

Committees for cases of sexual harrassment 
2744. SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Supreme Court has directed to constitute committees to look into the 
cases of sexual harassment in both the Central and State Government departments; 
261 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details of the Committees constituted so far, State-wise; 
(c) whether Government have noticed any lapse by any departments in 
constituting such committees; and 
(d) if so, the details thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI KANTI SINGH): (a) The 
Supreme court, in the judgement delivered in August, 1997 in the case of Vishaka 
and Others Vs. State of Rajasthan and Others, laid down norms and guidelines to 
be followed by the employees or other responsible persons in the workplaces 
or other institutions to prevent or deter the commission of acts of sexual 
harassment and to provide the procedures for resolution, settlement or 
prosecution of acts of sexual harassment by taking all steps required, including 
setting up of complaints committee to redress the complaint made by the 
victim. 
(b) The matter falls in the purview of the State Governments. 
(c) and (d) The National Commission for Women (NCW) has informed that 
according to the information which b ecame available during the interactive 
meetings held by it since November, 2000 with various organizations 
including State Government Departments, complaints committees had not 
been formed in a number of cases. Th e committee which existed did not have 
50% reservation for women. 
In July, 2004 and again in May, 2005, the Department of Women and Child 
Development emphasized to all Central Ministries/Departments and State 
Governments and Union Territory Administrations the need to ensure the setting up 
of complaints committee as per the guidelines laid down in the Supreme Court's 
judgement and their proper functioning.

2761. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that his minist ry has allocated separate funds for 
education of the challenged children; 
(b) if so, the amount thereof; and 
(c) the manner in which his Ministry is planning to spend it; the areas of the 
education to which the priority would be given? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) An amount of Rs. 45.00 Crores has been allocated for 2005-
06 under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Integrated Education for the 
Disabled Children (IEDC). 100% assistance is provided under various components of 
the scheme for education of children suffering from mild to moderate disabilities in 
common schools. The components include facilities for disabled children, 
educational aid3, assistive equipment and salaries for special teachers. Under the 
Inclusive Education component of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), an amount 
of Rs. 186.79 Crores have been allocated for 2005-06. The amount will be 
spent on various activities for the education of children with special needs in the 
6-14 years age group, viz. medical & functional assessment of their needs, 
preparing such children for schools, provision of aids and appliances, teacher 
training barrier free access to schools,  specialized resource support and 
appropriate teaching learning methodologies.

• State Governments have been asked for strict implementation of child

Child Development especially to target prevention of child marriages in the

(i) revision in rate of sumptuary allowance admissible to the Judges of Supreme 
Court and High Courts,

Courts—Revision of pension, family pension etc., of Judges of High Courts 
and Supreme Court.

Funds for Mumbai under National Urban Renewal Mission 
2858. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have announced setting up of National Urban Renewal 
Mission with a Rs. 5500 crore outlay in the year 2005-06;

THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
391 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
(b) A statement is enclosed (See below). 
(c) Funds under the Mission are not earmarked state-wise/city-wise. For accessing 
funds, cities are required to prepare 'City Development Plans' (CDPS) and 'Detailed 
Project Reports' (DPRS) and submit them for appraisal to the competent authorities 
prescribed under the scheme. Projects shall be funded after due appraisal and signing of 
tripartite agreement among the Central Government, State Government and the Urban 
Local Bodies/Parastatals. 
Statement 
Details of JNNURM and its objectives 
* The mission comprises two sub-missions, viz., Sub-Mission-I for Urban 
Infrastructure and Governance and sub-Mission-ll for basic Services for the 
Urban Poor. 
* The Mission provides focused attention to 63 select cities in different 
States. 
* For cities/towns not covered under the Mission, the Ministry of Urban 
Development has launched a scheme known as Urban Infrastructure 
Development Scheme for Small and Medium Towns (UIDSSMT) while the 
Ministry of Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation has formulated a scheme 
known as Integrated Housing and Slum Development Programme 
(IHSDP). 
* The following on-going schemes of the Ministries of Urban Development 
and Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation have been subsumed in 
JNNURM:— 
(i) Infrastructure Development in Mega cities. 
(ii) Integrated Development of Small & Medium Towns. 
(iii) Accelerated Urban Water Supply Programme. 
(iv) Urban Reform Incentive Fund 
* Provision of Central assistance is linked to implementation of 
certain mandatory as well as optional reforms at the State and 
ULB/Parastatal levels. 
392 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
* Implementation of all mandatory and optional reforms has to be completed 
during the Mission period of 7 years beginning from 2005-06. 
* Central assistance is in the form of 100% grant to be funded as Additional 
Central Assistance (ACA). 
* Cities have to prepare City Development Plans (CDPs) and Detailed 
Project Reports (DPRS). 
* 5% of the Central grant or actual requirement, whichever is less, is provided for 
preparation of City Development Plans, Detailed Project Reports, Capacity 
Building, Information, Education and Communication (IEC) activities 
etc. 
* Signing of Tripartite Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) by the State 
Governments and Urban Local Bodies/Parastatals with Central Government 
is a necessary condition to access Central funds. MoA should indicate 
commitments and milestones to be achieved in the implementation of reforms 
at the State & ULB/ Parastatals levels. 
*FINANCING PATTERN 
Depending upon population, geographical location of the cities and category to 
which a city belongs, fund is provided as indicated below:— 
(i) 35%/50%/80%/90% of the cost of projects would be funded by Govt. of 
India through 100% ACA and 
(ii) 65%/50%/20%/10% would be funded by State/ULBs/Financial Institutions. 
* Funds to be released in four installments. 
* First installment shall be released on signing of MoA and approval of City 
Development Plans (CDPs)/Detailed Project Reports (DPRs). 
* Release of subsequent installment to be linked to achievement of 
reform/milestones and progress of projects. 
OBJECTIVES OF JNNURM ARE: 
1. To provide focused attention to integrated development of 
infrastructural services in the cities. 
393 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
2. To secure effective linkages between asset creation and asset 
management so that the infrastructur al services created in the cities 
are not only maintained efficiently but also become self-sustaining 
over time. 
3. To ensure adequate investment of funds to fulfill deficiencies in the 
urban sector. 
4. To have planned development of identified cities including peri-urban 
areas, out growths, urban corridors. 
5. To scale up delivery of civic amenities and provision of utilities with 
emphasis on universal access to urban poor. 
6. To take up urban renewal programme, i.e., re-development of inner (old) 
cities area to reduce congestion.

Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY) is a demand driven Centrally sponsored scheme 
with 50:50 funding pattern between Centre and the States with the objective to facilitate 
construction and upgradation of dwelling units with sanitation facilities for the urban 
slum dwellers living below the poverty line including members of economically weaker

1. SC/ST — Not less than 50% 
2. Backward Classes — 30% 
3. Other weaker sections — 15% (OBC, BC, etc.) 
4. Physically disabled persons — 5%

The objective of Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan is to provide healthy and enabling urban 
environment through community toilets.

released to States during the last three years is given in the Statement (See below).

called Integrated Housing and Slum Development

The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council Bill, 2005 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
Sir, I beg to move: 
"That the Bill to provide for the creation of Legislative Council for 
the State of Andhra Pradesh and for matters supplemental, 
incidental and consequential thereto, as passed by Lok Sabha, 
be taken into consideration. 
Sir, The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council Bill, 2004, was 
introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16th December, 2004, and was passed 
by the Lok Sabha on 15th December, 2005. 
The Bill seeks to provide for the cr eation of Legislative Council in 
the legislature of the State of Andhra Pradesh for matters supplemental, 
incidental and consequential thereto. Article 169 of the Constitution of 
India provides that Parliament may by law provide, inter-alia, for the 
creation of the Legislative Council if  the Legislative Assembly of the 
State passes a resolution to that e ffect by majority of the total 
membership of the Assembly and by a majority of not less than two-
thirds of the members of the Assembly present and voting. The same 
article also contemplates that any such law may contain such 
supplemental, incidental, consequential provisions as Parliament may 
deem fit necessary. 
Sir, the Legislative Assembly of Andhra Pradesh had passed a 
resolution on 8th July, 2004 in terms of Article 169(1) of the 
Constitution for the creation of a Legislative Council in the State. In 
this connection, it may be submitted,  Sir, that the Legislative Council 
existed in the State of Andhra Pr adesh prior to 1985, which was 
abolished w.e.f. 1st June, 1985. Thereafter, on the basis of a resolution 
passed by the Andhra Pradesh Legislat ive Assembly for revival of the 
Legislative Council in the State, a Bill to the effect, containing a similar 
provision for the State of Tamil Nadu also, was introduced in 
454 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
the Rajya Sabha on 10.05.1990, and had been passed by that House 
on 28th May,  1995. 
This Bill, however, lapsed on the dissolution of the Ninth Lok 
Sabha, and the State of Andhra Pradesh, later, withdrew its request for 
the revival of the Council. The present Bill seeks to provide for 
creation of the Legislative Council in the State of Andhra Pradesh, with 
a total strength of ninety members, 31 of which are to be elected by the 
local authorities, eight each to be elected by the graduates and teachers 
constituencies; 31 by the Legislativ e Assembly; and, the remaining 
twelve are to be nominated by the Governor. The local authorities have 
been represented in the Legislative Council or the Municipal Corporation, 
Municipalities, Nagar Panchayats,  Cantonment Boards, Zilla Praja 
Parishads and Mandal Praja Parishads. The constitution of the Legislative 
Council is; therefore, the same as it  had existed prior to its abolition, 
except for the local bodies, constituting the local authorities' 
constituencies.

In this context, it may be added that the issue of providing voting rights 
to the primary school teachers in the Legislative Council has been under

of consensus among the concerned bodies... namely, the States having

Government, therefore, does not accept that recommendation of the 
Department-related Standing Committee to have a relook at the issue of 
enrolment of primary teachers in constituencies. Sir, with these words, I 
commend that this Bill may be taken into consideration.

that Resolution as per its rules of procedure. In 1996, the State 
Government had only said that it is not in favour of revival of the Legislative 
Council. That means, the Legislative Council of Andhra Pradesh has not 
been abolished as has been required under Article 169(1) of the Constitution 
and is only, if I may say so, under suspended animation. So, my point is, how 
can you create a new Legislative Council when there is a Resolution 
pending for revival and even if you want to revive, I failed to understand how can 
you revive a Legislative Council under Article 169(1) which allows you only to 
abolish or create a Legislative Council. That means, you are creating 
Legislative Council when there is already a Legislative Council—as it has 
not been abolished as per the rules of procedure. So, to my understanding, 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, this Bill is unconstitutional, unethical, against the 
rules of procedure and against the wishes of the people of Andhra Pradesh. 
Sir, the third point I wish to make is this. Even if you look at the 
Constituent Assembly Debates of Volume VII of 1948, there is no 
unanimity in favour of the State Legislative Councils. The arguments 
488 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
that have been put forth against having Legislative Councils are: It is not 
comprised of the representatives of the people as such, it is a protective armour 
for the vested interests, i.e., the ruling party, and that is a drag on the public 
exchequer. If you took at Article 197, the Legislative Councils have power 
only to delay mattes, and that too only for a limited time. If a Bill that is passed by 
the Assembly is rejected by the Council, the former can pass it again in the 
same form for transmission to the Council, and if it is again rejected, the Bill 
shall be deemed to have been passed by both the Houses. The other logic given 
by the Government of Andhra Pradesh is about giving representation to certain 
special functional interests such as local bodies, teachers, graduates, scholars, 
experts, etc: Sir, in our democratic set up, large emphasis is given on setting up 
of various fora, like the National In tegration Council, Citizens Peace 
Committees, Citizens Advisory Committees, etc., on subjects like health, legal aid, 
education, rural development, etc. So, these citizens are given representation in 
these bodies. Hence, the prominent citizens of the State have chance in 
these bodies to present their viewpoint. Sir, even Dr. Ambedkar, the Chairman 
of the Constitution Committee agreed to this. This becomes clear if you look at 
page 1309, dated 6th January, 1949, Volume-VII, 1948. With your permission, 
Sir, I just wish to quote what Dr. Ambedkar has said. He said, and I quote, "I don't 
think the view of those who are opposing the Second Chambers can be better put 
than in the words of Abbe Seiyes. His criticism was two-fold. He said that if the 
Upper House agrees with the Lower one, then it was superfluous. If it did not 
agree with the Lower House, it was a mischievous body and we ought not to 
entertain it. The first part of the Abbe Seiyes is, undoubtedly valid, because it 
is so obvious..."

Government, and appeal to all my hon. colleagues, to out-rightly reject this Bill 
and save money, and also, stop the creation of another political 
rehabilitation center. Thank you, Sir.

so urgent—purchasing of an aircraft that has been discussed by this House, 
which is under consideration of the Government— also to be done through

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, I am grateful to the hon. Members for their 
valuable comments on the Bill to replace the Ordinance. Let me begin, Sir, by 
expressing my regret that I was not here at 3.20 p.m. I was on my feet in the Lok 
Sabha and my colleague, Mr. Palanimanickam, was here. I came at about 
3.25 p.m. after the other Bill was passed. Sir, the first question, that is raised, is, 
Ordinances are never made, or, usually not made, especially, taxation 
Ordinances are not made. 
I have, Sir, a long list of Taxation Ordinances beginning from 1953. And if I 
confine myself to Kaul and Shakdher, I have to stop with 1996; there are a 
series of Ordinances. But, more interestingly, I have with me references of two 
Ordinances; one Ordinance was issued on the 3rd February 2001 levying 
surcharge; and the other Ordinance was issued on the 8th September 2003 
reducing the interest rate for calculating interest on delayed refunds. By these two 
Ordinances, the Government of the day

Firstly, Sir, I would hope that the former Finance Minister would extend 
the courtesy of listening to my Budget Speech as carefully as I listened to his

In paragraph 180 of my Budget Speech, I said, "I have received many 
suggestions on amendments to the direct tax laws and the indirect tax laws. I 
have decided to accept some suggestions that require to be acted upon 
immediately." And these are the crucial words, "But I do not propose to burden the 
Finance Bill with those changes. Instead, I intend to introduce a separate Bill 
for that purpose during this session." And that is the Bill, which I introduced and 
that is the Bill which is before the Standing Committee. Therefore, it was not 
an afterthought that we introduced the Bill to amend the tax laws. It was a

be burdened with other provisions. We, therefore, introduced two Bills. One 
was the Finance Bill, the traditional Finance Bill, and the other was the Taxation 
Laws (Amendment) Bill, which is before the Standing Committee. But after the 
Budget was passed, after the Finance Act was passed, and after the other Bill 
was referred to the Standing Committee, there have been some 
developments, which required an Ordinance. Again, this is not an 
afterthought. This is not shoddy workmanship. This is the compulsion of 
circumstances. I will do my best to give reasons why each circumstance was a 
compelling circumstance. And, of course, it is for the House to decide whether 
my justification of the circumstance is right or whether my learned friend's 
criticism, that there was no circumstance, is right That is for the House to 
decide. 
Let us begin, Sir, with Civil Avia tion, what is the position on Civil 
Aviation? In my Budget Speech, in paragraph 173,1 said, "In deference to the 
request from Air India and Indian Airlines, I propose to extend up to

The second amendment is on international sporting events. Now, Sir, 
the Budget was passed, the Finance Act was passed and Parliament got 
adjourned some time in the middle of may. The International Cricket Council 
decided that the World Cup event will be awarded to India. But they wanted a 
categorical assurance that the income arising out of that tournament will not 
be taxed in India. Now, this matter was discussed at several levels and 
finally, all of you know that the Chairman of the ICC and others met the Prime 
Minister. The Prime Minister assured them that he would consider giving a 
tax exemption, but they should make a formal written request, following the 
meeting. They made a request on the 21st May of 2005. And then, when they 
made a request on 21st May, 2005, we wrote back to them because it was on 
the eve of their meeting. On 31st May, 2005, we wrote back to them saying 
that under certain conditions, the income-tax exemption will be granted. So, 
this was after the Finance Act, after the Budget and if we have to attract that 
particular tournament to India, we were obliged to give this exemption. But 
the amendment that I am making are not confined to cricket. The amendment 
that I am making applies to all sporting events. It will apply to all multi-
countrysporting events where the international body has blessed that event 
as a recognised event which means, it will apply if, say, World Cup Football 
comes to India, as I hope it will come one day and will be played either in 
Kerala or in Goa or in Bengal. I hope so. I want to see

company being its holding company engaged in the business of generation 
or transmission or distribution of power and any income arising out of transfer 
of capital assets being an asset of an undertaking engaged in the business of 
generation or transmission or distribution of power, shall be exempt. It means, 
the parent company when it gives money to the subsidiary company, in the 
hands of the subsidiary company, that grant will be exempted from income-
tax and any transfer of capital assets from the erstwhile Dhabol Power Company 
to the Ratnagiri Gas and Power Company will also be exempt from capital 
gains tax. Similarly, we have introduced clause 5 whereunder section 80 (1 A)

Power Company in this case, with majority equity participation by public 
sector companies, for purposes of enforcing

Sir, Members are absolutely right, this is a big question: Is trading in 
a license an export profit? Now, cert ain sub-sections were introduced, 
and my friend, Mr. Yashwant Sinha, will recall that by the Finance Act of 
1990 I am not the author of that Act- ...  
That Government and that Minister, at that time, introduced section 
28(iiia), (iiib) and (iiic). It contemplated only sale of certain licences under 
the Imports Control Order and Imports and Exports Control Act, it 
contemplated cash assistance and it contemplated any drawback 
received. That was the export benefit available at that time. There was also 
clause (iv) which said, "the value of any benefit or perquisite, whether convertible 
into money or not, arising from business or the exercise of profession". This 
was the position. 
The DEPB was introduced in 1997-98. Now, I will answer Mr. 
Ramachandraiah why we are giving it retrospective effect from 1.4.1998. The 
DEPB was introduced in 1997-98. The first assessment year for DEPB 
benefit is, therefore, the assessment year beginning on 1.4.1998. Our friend, 
Mr. Yashwant Sinha, phased out 80HHC by 31.3.2005. Therefore, we are 
talking about a period from 1 -4-1998 to 31-3-2005. This problem did not arise 
for any period prior to 1.4.1998, nor does this problem arise after 
1.4.2005. We are talking about only this period. 
534 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
During this period, a question arose as to whether the sale of DEPB 
licence or more accurately, the transfer of a DEPB credit, would amount 
to export profit or not. The Department took the view that it is not export 
profit. I think, a very powerful argument can be made in a court of law 
that it is not export profit. Firstly, it  is not related to export at all. It is 
trading in a credit or a licence. Secondly, the compensation that you 
earn from that is not in foreign exchange; it is in Indian rupees. A powerful 
argument can be made. Equally on the exporters side, they argue that 
it falls under section 28(iiia), (iiib) and (iiic). Now, on a plain reading of 
section 28(iiia), (iiib) and (iiic), which I read out to you, it does not apply. 
It could not have applied because DEPB came after section 28(iiia), 
(iiib) and (iiic) was introduced. Now, what is the position? Some paid 
the tax and disputed it. Some did not pay the tax. This dispute was 
going on. One case, to which Mr. Sinha referred, which I referred to in 
the other House, and he has got the facts from there, went to the Income-
Tax appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal rejected both the cases. The Tribunal 
did not accept the case of the exporter, nor did it accept the case of the 
Department. It found a third reason and said, "because of this reason 
you can't apply Explanation (baa) to 80HHC", and, therefore, ultimately 
it ended up giving relief to the exporter not by accepting the argument of 
the exporter, but on some other argument. Obviously, against that order, 
the Department has gone on appeal to the High Court. Now, I have two 
courses open before me. I could have said, "very well, the matter is 
before the High Court. Let the High Court decide". The High Court will 
decide this case over a period of four  or five years, then it goes to the 
Supreme Court. One of us is bound to go to the Supreme Court because 
it involves a large amount of money. When we go to the Supreme Court, 
it will take another three or four year. Now, who will benefit. The lawyers 
will benefit. But the point is that the exporters will still be uncertain 
because for eight or nine years the question is not decided one way or 
the other. Therefore, when the exporters met us, met me, met the 
Commerce Minister, met the Prime Minister, we said, "all right, we will 
find a solution to the problem". It is not that we will be able to concede 
their entire case that everybody must be exempt or deny to everybody 
any benefit. We said, "we will look into the matter and we will find a 
golden mean". We referred it to the Economic Advisory Council. The 
Economic Advisory Council gave us a report. Four recommendations 
were made by the Economic Advisory Council and these are the four 
535 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
recommendations made by the Economic Advisory Council: 
"Accordingly, our recommendations are as follows: 
1. If the export turnover was Rs. 10 crores or less, the corresponding 
income-tax assessment may not be reopened and they may be 
given the benefit of exemption." 
I have accepted it. 
2. If the export turnover was more than Rs. 10 crores, the 
corresponding income-tax assessment may be reopened. If the 
exporter had claimed DEPB credit and also tax exemption for 
such DEPB credit under section 80HHC(3), the return may be 
reassessed without the benefit of exemption and additional tax 
may be levied." 
However, no such reassessment may be made till the exporter is able to 
prove that (a) he had a choice between drawback and DEPB for the given export 
product and (b) the customs component of the drawback rate was higher than the 
DEPB rate. I have accepted it. Third, no penalty by way of interest, penal interest 
should be levied. In other words, fresh demand should be limited to the actual 
tax payable. I have accepted it and we are issuing instructions and 
implementing this 'no penalty and no interest". Four, the arrears of tax on the 
basis of reassessment may be collected over two years, according to an 
instalment schedule, as may be decided by the IT Department. I have not 
only accepted it, I have said the arrears, if any, will be collected over five 
years, not two years. We have faithfully accepted the report of the Economic 
Advisory Council. Now a question was raised that a bulk of the exporters will 
not benefit. That is not correct. We have the number of exporters. By 
imposing a limit of Rs. 10crores, out of about 65,000 exporters, 61,000 
exporters are covered. It is only t he very large exporters who are not 
covered. Even they can get the exemption if they satisfy the two 
conditions. This is a golden mean that we have struck. I cannot give up 
revenues, nor do I wish to burden the small exporters on a matter which is 
clearly an arguable matter. I am not saying that the Department's case alone 
is arguable. The Departments' case is an arguable case and the exporter's case 
is an arguable case. But only one of them can win 
536 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and that too after eight or nine years. Therefore, we have adopted this method 
in order to give relief. I have received letters in the last few days after the Lok

These are important amendments to the Income Tax Act. A suggestion was 
made by Shri Soz that we should simplify the Income Tax Act. I entirely agree 
with him. In fact, in paragraph 180 of my Budget Speech, I had said that I intend

working on that. Five Working Groups have been set up. The reports will be 
received, hopefully, by the end of this month. I am confident, sometime, during 
the Budget Session, we will be able to place before the House the Income Tax 
Bill. I think it is very important for us to refine the income tax law. Too many 
people are exploiting the loopholes in the income Tax Act. The Income Tax Act 
has now become a playground for people to abuse the Income Tax Act and 
exploit the

SHRI KAMAL NATH: Sir, there are two types of checks which are done, one is 
the pre-despatch inspection and the other is the quality audit. Quality audit is over and 
above the pre-despatch inspection. As the name implies, pre-despatch inspection is pre-
despatch. Quality audit is carried out after the items or the products have been received by 
the consumers, that is, the buyer. That is done as a precautionary measure over and above, 
as the word implies, it is 'quality audit'. So, pre-despatch inspection is one part of it. That 
having been done, in about six per cent of the cases, as a matter of abundant caution, and, 
in cases where the stores are large or the items can be manipulated in despatch, then a 
quality audit is done. So, as the hon. Member asked about the quality audit, my 
response is regarding quality audit. But I would like to inform him that quality audit 
supersedes, that is, over and above, the pre-despatch inspection.

†*404. SHRI AJAY MAROO:ft 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn towards the incidents 
of rape, loot, dacoities and other criminal activities in trains in Jharkhand and 
other States; 
(b) whether there is any specific criteria to fix the responsibility in this 
matter; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) what measures have been taken for the safety of lives and property of 
passengers travelling by train? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PAUL): (a) 
to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.

(a) to (d) Government is aware abou t the incidents of dacoity, robbery,

Governments. A statement indicating nu mber of cases registered during the 
years 2003, 2004 and 2005 (up to June) is enclosed (See below). NCRB

RAJYA SABHA [21 December, 2005] 
"Police" and "Public Order" are state subjects under the seventh Schedule to the 
Constitution of India and therefore the primary responsibility for detection, 
registration, investigation and prosecution as well as prevention of crime lies with the 
State Governments. lncluding crime committed on running trains. With a view to provide 
better security to the travelling passengers in trains and passenger areas, the 
Government has taken the following measures: 
(i) The Railway Protection Force Act, 1957 and the Railways Act, 1989 have 
been amended to enable the Railways, through the Railway Protection Force 
(RPF), to effectively control crime on railways in collaboration with State 
Police Force. 
(ii) RPF has also been empowered to deal with minor offences affecting the train 
operations such as alarm, chain pulling, roof travel, touting, ticket-less 
travelling, unauthorized entry. 
(iii) RPF personnel are being deployed to escort many trains and they are also 
being deployed in the passenger area. 
(iv) Coordination meetings between railways and state police are held periodically 
to reivew remedial measures for prevention of crimes on railways, the 
position in the sections, trains and stations affected by crimes. 
(v) Whenever there is a flare-up of violent incidents in any section, all-out efforts 
are made in coordination with the state police to control the situation, by 
actively assisting them with additional man power and other resources.

(a) According to the Wastelands Atlas of India, published in 2005 by the

(b) and (c) The aim of wasteland development is to improve degraded and 
wastelands through efficient adoption of the principles of restoration, 
conservation and ecological balance. Accordingly, the guidelines for the area 
development programmes of the Department of Land Resources have been 
formulated on the wasteland approach. The activities under these programmes 
include soil and moisture conservation works, harvesting of rain water, 
afforestation, horticulture, floriculture, development of pasture lands, fisheries, 
etc. to generate employment in the rural areas. To check overuse of natural 
resources and to ensure its efficient management, the schemes have adopted 
the participatory approach encourages village communities towards sustained 
community action for the maintenance of assets created and promotes simple, 
easy and affordable technolgical su lutions. As these are demand driven 
schemes, funds are not allocated Stat e-wise. The funds released and area 
treated during the last three years under the area development programmes 
are given in enclosed Statement-ll.

under Entry No. 18 of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. State Governments 
distribute Government wastelands to the eligible landless rural poor. According 
to the reports received from the State Governments, an area of 147.47 lakh acres 
of Government wastelands has been distirbuted so far.
